Questions for Oral Answer—Transfer of Questions

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Before we get to questions, I want to raise with you a point of order that goes
to Speakers’ rulings 151/2 and 151/5-6, and to your ruling on 22 May, which has not yet
made it into the green book.
Mr Speaker, you have given Opposition me mbers in particular some good advice
over a period of time regarding making ques tions specific and clear if we expect
Ministers to be prepared to answer them . This morning the Labour Opposition lodged a
question to the Prime Minister that asked whether he stood by his statements that he and
his Ministers had made in relation to the Reading Recovery question—that is, whether
the Prime Minister stands by his statement. Th at goes to what is in the Prime Minister’s
mind and his opinion. Speaker’s ruling 151/2 does make it clear that there is an ability
to transfer, as we all know, but I raised with you, through your office, the question of
whether Speakers’ ruling 151/5 might apply in this case, as to whether it was possible
for another Minister to indi cate what was in the Prime Minister’s mind and who has
responsibility for that. I will get back to that point in a second.
The next draft of the question that cam e back from the Government—it was a
proposal to shift it to the Minister of Education—asked whether she stands by her
statements and those of the Prime Minister. That is clearly a very different question. It is
not a question about whether the Prime Minister stood by his statements; it is a question
as to whether that Minister stood by hers and agreed with the Prime Minister, which is
quite different. I think we would all accept that  no junior Minister could be responsible
for what is in the Prime Minister’s mind. It then moved along to whether she had been
informed whether the Prime Minister stands by his statements in relation to this, and
that is the question that appears on the Order Paper.
Mr Speaker, the point that I would like to take you back to is your ruling on 22 May,
where I think you gave some very good advice to, I think, Dr Norman on that particular
occasion. You said, in the case of a question to the Prime Minister, that had the member
simply asked the Prime Minister whether he stood by his statement with regard to asset
sales etc., and then stopped the question, the member’s point would have had merit. We
took on your advice from that. We did not as k about ministry advice, we did not ask
about any other related matters, and we submitt ed a question in that format, because we
thought that at that po int it would not be possible—it is  a direct questi on. Obviously, it
is a matter of public knowledge that the Prim e Minister is not here, but we have an
Acting Prime Minister. It is our view that it becomes a farce if this Parliament—if
Opposition members of this Parliament—ca nnot ask the Prime Minister whether he
stands by his statements made about a partic ular issue in the very  recent past. That is
why I indicated to the Clerk’s Office, for you, that I thought that this could well be a
case for Speaker’s ruling 151/5, because we ar e getting to the poi nt where it becomes
almost impossible to hold the Government to account, to hold the Prime Minister to
account for what he says, if, in  fact, questions are transferre d in this way. I can accept
that in a lot of areas it can be appropriate to transfer th em, but my submission to you,
Mr Speaker, is that it is not possible for any ot her Minister to be responsible for what is
5122 Points of Order 12 Sep 2012
in the Prime Minister’s mind, and, therefore, this goes to  the type of question for which
transfer should not be allowed.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I think two things are relevant
here. Firstly, the question was to do with  Reading Recovery, and with comments by
other Ministers as well. Secondly, we do not ab use the process, and I reject completely
the suggestion by the shadow Leader of the House that we do. Transferring the question
to the Minister of Education, particularly  on a day when it is plain and evident to
everybody that the Prime Minister himself is not  in the country, let alone in the House,
would have given a better opportunity for th e information that the Opposition clearly
wanted around Reading Recovery to be pr operly discussed. The questions never stop
with just the question: “Do you stand by all your statemen ts? Yes, I do; end of the
question.” They do not. They carry on through the supplementary question process,
where further information is sought, presumably and usually about the issue that is
identified as part of that que stion. In transferring the question to the Minister, we were
simply wanting to create an opportunity for more information to be more authoritatively
given to the House.
But what I would say also is that the question that now appears on the Order Paper is,
I think, a little on the tough side. I can see now how we got to this, because both parties
would appear to be somewhat unhappy about the question. But I think, rather than going
into the merits of the question and how we got there, I would like to just leave my
contribution strongly at the fact that we are not trying to frustrate the process at all.
You have been very, very strong over th e past few years—the last 4 years—in
requiring Ministers to answer questions and to provide information to the House. You
have pulled many of us up, in cluding me, for not giving en ough information. That is a
consideration that we always have in mind when we look at whether or not a question
should be transferred. In this circumstance,  with Mr Mallard’s own comments that no
other Minister could know what was on the mind of th e Prime Minister, it seems
somewhat ridiculous to be s uggesting that the transfer was inappropriate when, in fact,
the information itself could never be directly solicited.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Speaking very briefly to
that—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear very briefly further from the honourable shadow Leader
of the House.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: There are two points. The first is that it is well
established in the Speakers’ rulings that the absence of a Minister is not the reason for
the transfer. It is a matter of responsibility, not presence, and therefore I think part of the
response from the Leader of the House fails. But if it was a matter of having a Minister
who might be more informed than the person currently acting for the Prime Minister in
responding to the question, but keeping the ques tion the same, it is always an option for
the Government to have, in the absence of th e Prime Minister, another Minister actually
answer on his behalf. That might have been the logical and fair thing to do.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have allowed this point of orde r to take some time because I think
it is a serious issue for the House. I think the Hon Trevor Mallard has raised an
interesting dilemma for the House about question time. The fact that New Zealand does
not have a Prime Minister’s question time makes our question time a little different
from, say, that of the British Parliament. Th e dilemma that we all face in this—and I
think the honourable Leader of the House referred to this in  his response to the point of
order—is that where a question is whether th e Prime Minister stands by statements and
other Ministers’ statements, say, in relation to a specific issue, if the Government is
assuming that that issue is of the main interest to the questioner, the risk is that if it stays
with the Prime Minister, the Prime Minister , in answering, will say that the member
12 Sep 2012 Points of Order 5123
should put down a question to the relevant  Minister. That is why I think the
Government is not trying to, in my unde rstanding, escape accountability in trying to
make sure the substance of the issue can best be covered by the relevant Minister.
But I accept that it may not be that way. The questioner may, in fact, wish to be
pursuing something very much specific to th e Prime Minister’s statement, but that will
not automatically be obvious from the quest ion. That is the dilemma. The Government
is absolutely entitled to transfer a que stion, unless it would be anathema to
accountability for that to be the case. The member has raised that point, and I agree with
him that were the Prime Minister to be  the only person who could possibly have
information on a certain issue, then the que stion should not be tr ansferred. Where an
opinion is being sought, the bar is not quite at the same le vel, I would suggest, because
an opinion is never quite as important an accountability issue as where the Prime
Minister is being questione d on whether or not something happened. And if the Prime
Minister is the only person who could possibly know that, then  it would be contrary to
accountability in this House for such a question to be transferred.
We are in something of a dilemma. As Sp eaker I am in something of a dilemma in
handling this. I absolutely s upport the Government’s right to  transfer questions. What I
would like to suggest for the longer term, perhaps, is that the Standing Orders
Committee give some thought to whether or no t this House would like to set aside any
time during a parliamentary session for que stions to the Prime Minister. Other
Parliaments do have them. That may get over th is problem. That is something I leave in
members’ minds. I cannot see us easily resolv ing the issue with our current Standing
Orders, because the Speaker cannot possibly know the intention of the questioner when
they put the question down—whether they intend to go into the substance of a matter or
to stick just with the opinion as to whether the Prime Minister stands by any statements.
Opinions certainly are not matters that would prevent a question from being transferred.
There is no way, in my view, that we should allow the House to set a standard that a
question cannot be transferred just when an opinion is being sought.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I
want to raise with you just two issues. The fi rst is just to touch on the last point you
made, which is that I think it  is unreasonable for the Govern ment to transfer a question
based on where it thinks the Opposition is likely to be going with the question, rather
than on where the primary question itself goe s. The primary questi on in this case was
quite specific to the Prime Minister’s comments on a particular issue.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: And all his Ministers.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Well, it is a point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Chris Hipkins.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: So the issue we have is that  I think the public, quite rightly,
expect the Leader of the Opposition to be as king the Prime Minister questions about his
comments on a whole range of issues. And wher e the Prime Minister refuses to answer
the question by transferring it to another me mber, the public, rightly, will think that
Parliament is becoming a farce. It is not unr easonable to expect that the Prime Minister
will be answering questions from the Leader  of the Opposition about comments he has
made in public.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I hear what the member is saying, but the obvious problem in the
argument being put forward is that one assume s that members are actually interested in
the substance of the issues—one  assumes that. As soon as th e questioner gets into the
substance of the issue, the Prime Minister is absolutely at liberty to say that the member
should put down a question to the relevant Minister. That has happened, and it has
caused points of order to be raised in recen t weeks on that very issue, because it was
alleged that the Prime Minister had not an swered the question. The Prime Minister is
5124 Points of Order 12 Sep 2012
absolutely at liberty to make the point that  if members want detailed information on a
particular issue, the question should be referred to that Minister. The Government is
absolutely entitled to transfer questions unl ess the Prime Minister or the Minister to
whom the question is addressed is the only person who could possibly have information
of significance. Opinions about whether peop le stand by certain statements are hardly
matters that reach that test, in my view. It is only in recent year s that questions have
been allowed to cover opinions, and I am not about to see the bar raised on opinions to a
situation where questions th at seek opinions cannot be transferred. Disallowing the
transferral of a question must be  restricted only to issues of real significance, where the
Prime Minister or the Minister to whom th e question is being addressed is the only
person who could possibly have that information.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: I raise a point of order,
Mr Speaker. I wonder whether I can make an observation about these matters, because I
was here and Phil Goff was here in 1981, and I know that over recent years these
Standing Orders and procedural matters around question time have been changed—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: But the point I make is this: question time in this House is
now, for interested observers like myself and the public that sit here every day listening,
a shambles. It does the Parliament no good—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: —and I suggest—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. Order! It is not a point of or der. It is not a point of order to
go down that track.
Question No. 1 to Minister

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: In light of your decision regarding
that question, Mr Speaker, I am now faced with  a question that is very, very different
from the one I actually began with. My feeling, th erefore, is that if I am not able to ask
the Prime Minister or the Acting Prime Mini ster the question I originally intended and
to hold him to account, I respectfully withdraw my question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the member is entitled to do that. Question No. 2, Dr Russel
Norman. [ Interruption] Order! I have called Dr Russel Norman. [ Interruption] Now,
look. This nonsense will stop. I have acknowle dged that we have an issue here, and I
think it is worth giving further attention to this issue. I have suggested a way forward on
this issue. But I have now called Dr Russel Norman for question No. 2.
Children—Prime Minister’s Statements
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement, “The Government wants all young New Zealan ders to have the
opportunities they need to succeed and reach their full potential”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has he seen the Cabinet pape r on the social obligations for
parents policy that states that 2,200 parents wi ll have their benefits cut in the first year,
and how does that help their children reach their full potential?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I understand that that is not actually what the Cabinet paper
says. But I think that parents’ knowledge of those obligations means they are likely to
12 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5125
comply with them, precisely so that they do not put the welfare of their children at risk.
In fact, if they meet those obligations, it will be positive for their children.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to ta ble the Cabinet paper that shows that 2,200
parents will have their benefits cut in the first year.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that the Cabinet paper sp ecifies that only “the most
disadvantaged and vulnerable beneficiary families will be tested for complying with the
regime”, what will happen to their kids once their parents’ income is slashed?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government takes the view that almost all of those
parents will understand that they are reas onable obligations, because they are not so
much obligations to the Government, they are obligations to their own children. We
believe that most parents—in fact, almo st all parents—would comply with those
obligations.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that the Cabinet pape r itself admits that around 2,200
parents will not comply with th e obligations and hence will ha ve their benefit cut, is it
really moral for the Government to punish children for the perc eived sins of their
parents?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In the first place, let us get it clear that it would be the
parents who are punishing their children, not the Government. Secondly, we take a
more optimistic view than the officials’ view in the Cabinet paper. The Prime Minister’s
view is that most parents—in fact, almost all parents—are likely to comply with those
obligations, and that means better results for their children.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why does the Minister continue  to make the point, to argue,
that parents—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: What’s going on here?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Is the member calling a point of order?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: No, I am asking a question. It is called question time.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry. I beg the member’s pardon, but I did not see him stand and I
called Dr Russel Norman.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that the Cabinet paper itself says that around 2,200
parents will not meet the requ irements of this policy and wi ll hence have their incomes
slashed by the Government, does he take responsi bility for the fact that the children of
those parents will go hungry because his Government will cut their income by 50
percent?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I believe that the presence of the sanction will encourage
almost all parents, except maybe those who are completely reckless in their regard for
their own children, to comply with the obligations. It is an obligation to their children in
the first place, and in the second place to th e taxpayers, who are providing almost all of
the income on which those families are living.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why is the Prime Minister able to stand by his statement as
outlined in question No. 2 today, but not stand by his statement as outlined in question
No. 1 today? What is the difference here?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The difference is that he was not asked question No. 1.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. He most certainly was
asked question No. 1, which related to all the statements he—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I have not finished yet.
5126 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have heard sufficient. [ Interruption] Order! The member will
resume his seat. We are both of advanced ye ars, but we can move a little quicker than
that. The question on the Order Paper today wa s not to the Prime Minister, and that is
the end of the matter as far as this House is concerned. The Minister’s answer was
perfectly proper.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. With respect, the
original question that went in from the l eader of the Labour Pa rty was to the Prime
Minister. That has been clea rly established. It was then changed, and then withdrawn. I
am making the point that the primary question that first came to the Prime Minister,
question No. 1, which was to do with a statement, as in question No. 2, is in fact,
therefore, the same. Therefore, why is he able to answer question No. 2 today, and not
question No. 1 as originally asked?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Minister’s answer was a perfectly fair answer because
question No. 1 today is to the Minister of Education. If the member wants to dig deeper,
he has further supplementary questions. But I cannot say to the Minister answering it:
“Minister, you mustn’t give that kind of answer. You must actually interpret the
member’s question as meaning this.” I cannot do that. The Minister answers the
question he hears, and he gave a perfectly fair answer to the question he heard. There
are further supplementary questions for the me mber to challenge that , and I am sure he
is perfectly capable of that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. First of all, is there
something going on here where the person in  control of the sound system decides
unilaterally that he himself will stop the conversation here? That has clearly been
perceived outside this House. It is not a laughing matter; it is serious.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! When I get to my feet I think they know that members are
meant to cease speaking and resume their seats, and I suspect they are being helpful to
members because if they do not do that they may not remain in the House that much
longer. It has been a practice for some tim e that when Speakers are dealing with a
matter, the member whose microphone was on has it switched off.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Am I to understand
that that is a directive that the sound system  controller is in charge of—that he got a
directive saying that, or he just worked it out for himself?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Had the member been around during recent years he would
have found that it has been a practice that has been going on for some time. I have not
directed them whatsoever to do it. I think it  is a practice that ha s developed to assist
with the order in the House so that me mbers can hear the Speaker and not other
members when the Speaker is delivering rulings to the House.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. With respect, it is not
the job of that man there, or woman, or whoever he is, to make those—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat right away. I will not
tolerate this nonsense any more. It is the Sp eaker’s responsibility to maintain order in
this House, and the member is just trifling w ith the Chair. I have invited the member to
carry on his line of questioning. He has got s upplementary questions that he can ask the
Minister. If he wants to pursue a matter of interest, he should do that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You are saying that
we have got supplementary questions to clea r this up, but the problem is that we have
all got limited supplementary questions he re. I have a question at No. 11 and every
supplementary question I use trying to find out  what happened here, I have lost when I
come to question No. 11. That is surely not an  answer. What I want to know is, first of
all, whether or not the Acting Prime Minister  was prepared to admit that the question
first came to the Prime Minister when it wa s put in this morning at 10.30. That is the
12 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5127
fact that I am trying to get out, and I s hould not have to wast e five supplementary
questions to get to a specific fact on that matter. It was a very clear question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I accept the member’s right to ask the question, absolutely,
but the question the Minister hears is the que stion the Minister is obliged to answer.
That is why we have supplementary questi ons. I accept the member’s point that there
are limited numbers, but it is a matter of what is most im portant to the right honourable
gentleman. The member has to focus on what is most important and use the questions as
he sees fit. But I cannot say to a Minist er answering a question: “Look, the questioner
really wanted this answer or meant that.”  I cannot do that. That would be wrong for the
Speaker to be doing that. I have to try to insi st that Ministers answer the questions they
hear. The Minister answered the question he heard.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that his earlier answers ac knowledged that there will be
some parents—possibly up to 2,200—who will have their benefit cut as a result of this
policy, how can it possibly be ethically accep table to punish the children of those
parents because the Government does not like the actions of those parents?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The point of the policy is to ensure that the parents take
actions that are consistent with better pros pects for their children in the first place and
that, secondly, they meet th eir obligations to the broade r community, which is offering
support for that family. The Government is  planning to introduce sanctions, as the
member has pointed out. Those are fairly r obust sanctions and the relevant department
would ensure that every option is given to the parents to enable them to meet their
obligation in the first place.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia ora t ātou katoa. Does the Prime
Minister agree that the $6.5 million negotiated in Budget 2011 by Māori Party Ministers
to expand family-based literacy program mes to all decile 1, 2, and 3 schools is a
positive step towards allowing those young New Z ealanders in those deciles to have the
opportunity they need to succeed and reach their full potential?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, and a feature of those programmes is precisely that the
parents learn alongside the children . It is consistent with the M āori Party’s general line
on policy in this respect: it prefers to discourage dependency and encourage
independence if at all possible, and the mean s of doing that should be consistent with
the values of whānau rather than the individuals concerned.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: If the principal reason that the Minister is giving behind this
policy is that parents in receipt of Govern ment support should be obliged to send their
children to preschool and other requirement s, then why will he not make the same
demands of parents in receipt of Working fo r Families, given that they also are in
receipt of Government support?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In some respects it is a matter of the practicality of operating
this kind of policy. It is simply going to be quite a challenge to operate it for all parents
on benefits, let alone parents who are in work. But, second ly, all the indicators show
that once a family has work income coming into the household, almost all the indicators
for children improve significantly. That is wh y the other, complementary part of this
policy, alongside social obligations, is activ e intervention by Govern ment to help these
families get into work, and strong encouragement for them to get into work.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Will he commit to a Government obligation to guarantee that every
child has a place in early childhood educati on and free doctors’ visits, no matter where
they live?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, in the first place, if there is not  an early childhood
education place immediately available, of c ourse parents cannot be sanctioned for not
meeting that obligation. [ Interruption] Well, we do not need  a guarantee, because
5128 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Sep 2012
actually, with growing demand, the early childhood sector will respond as it always has
and more places will be available.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Mr Speaker—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear Dr Russel Norman’s question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: What kind of a monstrous Government punishes children
because it does not like the actions of their parents, and is not this Government policy—
to paraphrase Exodus—a policy of laying th e alleged sins of the parents upon their
children?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I would ask the question of what kind of a monstrous
Government, of which the Greens were a part up to 2008, did absolutely nothing—
absolutely nothing—for the most vulnera ble children and the most impoverished
families in this country.
Denis O’Rourke : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The answer given by the
Minister was not an answer to the question that was asked.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member must resume hi s seat—the member must. I just
invite him to go and read the Hansard. The question asked was somewhat provocative
and the answer given was somewhat provocative, but that is the way it works.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he believe that access to the Reading Recovery programme is
important for ensuring all young New Zealanders are able to succeed and reach their
potential?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: For some young children that is the case. For some children,
actually, Reading Recovery does not work ; maybe they need access to other
programmes. But, in the end, the measure of  it is what those ch ildren are able to
achieve, and that is why it is hard to understand the confused Labour Party policy,
which cannot decide whether it supports measures of child achievement or not.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he agree with the Hon Bill English that “Reading Recovery is
a safety net for children w ho are struggling, but half of this country’s lower decile
schools, for whatever reason, are not making use of it.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, he does agree with him—the statement was made, I
think, 6 or 7 years ago. The member advises the Prime Minister that the reason that a lot

Economic Programme—Job Creation and Productivity
3. JONATHAN YOUNG (National—New Plymouth)  to the Minister of Finance:
What is the Government doing to in crease jobs and suppor t a productive and
competitive economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has taken a number
of quite significant measures to help businesses employ more people and pay them
more. The 90-day trial period for new employees has created 13,000 jobs. Business tax
in New Zealand has been held to 28c in  the dollar—lower than Australia’s—so
businesses retain more of their profits to inve st in their business. ACC levies have been
reduced this year by $600 million, reducing co sts to business. And the Government has
removed 170 unnecessary and excessive regul ations, saving an estimated $200 million
in compliance costs for businesses.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: How has the New Zealand ec onomy and employment market
performed over the last 2 years, and what is the outlook for the next few years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Prior to the last 2 years, of course, with the global financial
crisis in 2008 and 2009, there was a sharp rise  in unemployment. In the past 2 years,
however, almost 60,000 net new jobs have been created, and 150,000 new jobs are
forecast over the next 4 years. The after- tax average wage is up by 20 percent since
5130 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Sep 2012
2008. The everyday cost of living is increasing at  its slowest rate in 12 years. Interest
rates are at the lowest levels in 45 year s, saving a family with a $200,000 mortgage
$200 a week compared with 4 years ago. And we would expect, consistent with the
Budget 2012 forecasts, that economic growth of 2 to 3 percent will continue this
success.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he agree with Fitch Ratings  that the forecast widening in
the current account deficit and the high New Zealand dollar pose a risk to New Zealand;
if so, does he think he needs to do something about it?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, but I do not believe that the answer to it is a 20 percent
devaluation in the exchange rate, as advo cated by those Opposition parties. It is not
clear even how they would do it, even if they want to do something that is a bit odd.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: How is the Government supporting people to move from welfare
into work?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We need to take th e opportunity in a growing job market to
assist people from welfare into work. In  Budget 2012 and over the next few years the
Government will be investing around $500 million in welfare reforms. Current
programmes include the $62 million Job Streams package for wage subsidies, $55.1
million for 155 dedicated Work and Income staff to support job seekers and sole parents
looking for work, $80 million for early childhood education childcare and the
guaranteed childcare assistance payment, and $150 million for youth services, including
wraparound support for young people not in education, employment, or training.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Are record numbers of New Zealanders leaving for Australia
because his programme to increase jobs and improve the New Zealand economy is
working, or are they leaving because his G overnment has let them down and failed to
achieve the promises made when it was elected in 2008 and again in 2011?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think a number have been leaving because Australia has
experienced a once-in-100-year s terms of trade boost, wh ich has meant it has been
getting record prices for commodities and paying very high wages to dig those
commodities out of the ground. In more recen t months those commodity prices have
dropped off, and Australia may become a less attractive option. In fact, in the next 12
months New Zealand is likely to grow just as fast as, if not faster than, Australia.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: What recent reports has he seen  on jobs and grow th in the New
Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There have been a number of  reports about jobs, including
jobs that have been lost and new jobs that have been created. But the Manpower
Employment Outlook Survey, a survey of 650 employers, which was released earlier
this week, found that 27 percent intend to incr ease hiring, and 8 percent plan to reduce
hiring. When we have got relatively moderate  growth rates, some businesses and some
sectors will be doing well while others, as we have seen in the last couple of weeks, will
be doing poorly. But, on average, the economy is producing more jobs.
Emissions Trading Scheme—Proposed Changes
4. GRANT ROBERTSON (D eputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Climate Change Issues

Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Associate Mini ster for Climate Change Issues)  on
behalf of the Minister for Climate Change Issues : No. New Zealand remains on track
to meet its first commitment period obligations under the Kyoto Protocol to maintain its
average emissions at 1990 levels during the period 2008 to 2012. In fact, New Zealand
is expected to exceed its commitment.

Welfare Reforms—Investment Approach
5. Hon TAU HENARE (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : How
will the Government’s investment approach refocus New Zealand’s welfare system?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Mr Speaker—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear the answer.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Today we have announced further detail on the
Government’s investment approach to welf are. Our reforms will fundamentally change
the way welfare is delivered. We are appl ying an investment approach to understand
where best to target support, looking at each  individual on a benefit, given their needs,
challenges, and prospects of a quick return to  work. To do this, we tasked experts to
undertake an actuarial valuation of the welf are system, which shows us the different
types of benefits and the e ffect of policy changes on indi viduals within the benefit
system.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What does the valuation show about the costs of different types of
benefits?
5132 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The valuation shows that the lifetime cost of New
Zealand’s current benefit population is $78 billion. This reinforces exactly why we have
got to invest in people th rough a work focus system—so th at they do not get caught in
the trap of long-term welfare dependency.  The valuation tells us that those on
unemployment benefits represent just 5 percent of the lifetime cost of welfare—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What a waste of money!

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: —the angrier you get, the le ss likely you are to win the
argument, but that is fine—yet currently they  receive the lion’s sh are of support to get
them off welfare and into work, compared with sole parents at 23 percent, those on
sickness benefits at 9 percent, and those on invalids benefits at 24 percent.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Trying to look busy. Doing nothing about jobs, trying to look busy.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Opposition members call out, but, actually, although the
unemployment benefit did drop under them, we  saw the sickness benefit increasing, we
saw the invalids benefit increasing, and actually  they should be ashamed of what they
did for those people in that time.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How does the valuation support th e Government’s changes to the
welfare system to date?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Well, the valuation confirms that our changes to date are
focused on the right groups. The group with the highest individua l lifetime cost on
welfare is those who go on benefits before th e age of 18. The valuation shows that just
4,000 16 and 17-year-olds on benefits account fo r $1 billion of the lifetime cost. This
underlines why the Government’s first stage of welfare reforms was rightly focused on
ensuring young people do not become welfare dependent.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Has anything changed since the Ministry of Social Development in
a similar exercise roughly 18 months ago told us that to save money we should invest in
the young, the unwell, parents, and those on bene fits for longer periods; if not, what has
the Australian company Taylor Fry told her that she did not already know?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Actually, the valuation has given us a lot of things that
we did not know. It has taken at least 40 different models of analysing the system, and
has come up with a robust piece of data. It has taken more than 20 years of behaviours
of beneficiaries to come up with something that will actually give more transparency, or
accountability, actually, to New Z ealanders on what is worki ng, and what is not, over a
long period of time.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she confirm that in the ne xt year supera nnuation will cost
twice as much per annum as all main benefits  combined; if so, why will she not address
the cost and sustainability of this scheme, or  is this about costi ng what is politically
convenient?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I presume that the member is taking that information in
part from the actuarial that was done today that she is now dissing. The facts are that we
need to do projections so that  we can look at where the spe nd really is. I do not have a
crystal ball to tell me exactly what is going to happen with benefits, but with the right
sorts of interventions we can bring them down and see better resu lts for those people
who need them.

Science and Manufacturing Funding—2012 Science Investment Round Grants
7. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Science and

items.text: Today I announced

organisations have been awarded research  grants in the high-value manufacturing
sector. The 31 projects range from medical technologies like early  cancer detection to
nanotechnology insulation and cryogenic refr igeration. The $92 million for the projects

Employment’s 2012 science investment round, and follows the $133 million in science

co-funding for business. In addition to that, in July the Prime Mi nister and I announced

help hi-tech and high-value manufacturing firms become more competitive and get New
Zealand’s best ideas out of the lab and in to the market place faster. Legislation to
establish the Advanced Technology Institute wa s tabled in the House this week, and we
are hoping it will receive its first reading shortly.
