items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I move, That the House take note of
miscellaneous business . In a world increasingly dominated by debt, deficits, and
demonstrations, this is a Government that is protecting New Zealanders and growing the
economy. Nothing is more important to New Zealanders today th an a strong economy,
because that is where the jobs come from, that is where the independence comes from,
and that is where security for our families comes from—a strong, growing economy.
That is where top-quality he alth and education services come from. So this is a
Government focused on the economy. This is  not a Government focused on trivial,
electoral fluff like taking GST off food, free this, and free that. This is a Government
that is backing the producers of New Zeal and to get the economy moving for all. We
have cut taxes. We have got the lowest inte rest rates that we need. We have got low
inflation. This Government has reduced comp liance costs. We heard earlier on from the
Hon Steven Joyce, I think, that we ha ve removed 170 unnecessary and excessive
regulations from the law book. There is an unprecedented amount of progress on free-
trade agreements around the world. This Gove rnment has tidied up the capital markets,
and made a huge investment in innovation.
This Government has been dedicated to protecting New Zealanders from the sharp
edges of the recession, and the increasingly serious global financial crisis and worsening
international debt situation. The latest Eu ropean GDP quarters results stand in strong
contrast to the performance here in the New Zealand economy, especially when it
comes to the debt crisis that Europe is slidi ng further and further into. In the last quarter
New Zealand grew about 1 percent. You just  need to compare that with a negative
growth rate across Eu rope in that period. Germany, Sp ain, Italy, France, and Portugal
all had negative growth rates. In the last four of five quarters France has had a zero
growth rate. The Socialist President, elect ed on a platform of spend, spend, spend, has
just told the French people that he is now embarking on a programme of cut, cut, cut. So
the French have got their debt out of contro l. Every week we are seeing the evidence on
our television screens of how serious the im pacts of economic stagnation or decline are
in Europe, where even countries like Germany are facing these problems.
But here in New Zealand, with a balanced approach of control on spending and a
focus on value for money, and a determination to reduce the deficit,  control debt, and
improve public services, New Zealand is being able to deliver for its people. In fact, a
report released on Tuesday overnight from the OECD says that this Government spends
more of its Budget on education than any of the other 33 countries in the OECD. So we
are right up there. We will not comment about  the Opposition: it has spent the last 10
years saying there is nothing wrong with the New Zealand education system, and all of
a sudden we need Reading Recovery. It said there is nothing wrong with the New
Zealand education system, but all of a sudden we need Reading Recovery.
Let us focus just on what the OECD has actually said about the New Zealand
education system and the spending from this Government in the toughest of times. The
OECD says that New Zealand directed, in the latest year available,  over 21 percent of
its public spending to educat ion. That was enough to push us beyond the previous
bigger spender, Mexico, by nearly 1 percent. The OECD average is 13 percent. The
report also considers public spending on education as a proportion of GDP. Again, New
Zealand ranks highly with 7.2 percent, exceeded only by Sweden, Norway, Denmark,
12 Sep 2012 General Debate 5143
and Iceland. That is a major achievement  for New Zealand. In health, the average
OECD country had a zero increase in the ye ar under review, whereas New Zealand had
the second-highest increase of public commitment to health services in the OECD.
So, in a world increasingly dominated by de bt, deficits, and demonstrations from
upset voters, this Government is protec ting New Zealanders a nd growing the economy,
and every day we can see a Government that  is determined to work hard for New
Zealanders.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Tomorrow New Zealand First is releasing a
report from Business and Economic Research  summarising the case for amending the
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act. The Business and Economic Research report
concludes that New Zealanders’ lives will benefit from an amended Reserve Bank of
New Zealand Act. In alignment with the Business and Economic Research report, there
is now a broad consensus on the need for an amendment to the Reserve Bank of New
Zealand Act. The International Monetary Fund, exporters, manufacturers, many leading
economists and commentators, and even our own Reserve Bank are all agreed.
No serious economist will deny that our exch ange rate is overvalued, but yesterday
in this House, when the Minister of Fina nce was asked whether he agreed with the
overwhelming weight of expert opinion on the overvalued dollar, he fudged it. Today in
this House he fudged it once again. I quote th e Minister’s comment yesterday: “We do
agree with their level of discomfort about the high level of the New Zealand dollar,”. So
that is all right then, is it? It is all righ t that there is a level of discomfort, and the
Minister even today cannot disc lose or give us any more information on how that level
of discomfort is out there.
“Discomfort” is such a nice word—an inoffensive and euphemistic word. But ask the
workers in Kawerau, ask the workers in Bluff,  and ask the workers in Timaru, in South
Auckland, and throughout New Zealand who have  lost their jobs because the business
they work in no longer is competitive due to an overvalued dollar if they are
experiencing “discomfort”. Are they experi encing “discomfort”? Mo st certainly they
are. If you ask them that question, you will get a very blunt answer.
The plain fact is that the current Rese rve Bank of New Zealand Act is seriously
flawed. The focus on inflation is having a dire impact on New Zealand’s international
competitiveness. The current Act dates from 1989—a whole different epoch. The
fixation on a narrow inflation target may have been appropriate in the past but is now
creating a major headwind in the form of an overvalued New Zealand currency, creating
a great competitive disadvantage for our economy. Globally, inflation is not the threat it
was back in 1989.
Today we face a different threat to our economy: cut-throat competition in our export
markets, the very basis of our survival as  a developed, trading na tion. What the current
Act has given us is a chronica lly overvalued exchange rate, and the result is that every
week businesses are closing, markets are in jeopardy, and jobs are being lost. The New
Zealand public is now asking w hy there is no urgency, why there is no action from this
Government, and why there is no resolve.
The basic economics are straightforward. Our currency should reflect New Zealand’s
economic fundamentals. Instead, we have a pe rsistently overvalued exchange rate. That
has served the interests of international curr ency speculators—the so-called carry trade,
the people from the likes of Merrill Lync h and other money traders—who have done
well out of trading currency in this c ountry. Our overvalued exchange rate has
encouraged people to park money here simply to earn higher interest rates. That has led
to all manner of distortions. The facts and consequences of an overvalued exchange rate
are not in doubt. The facts on the ground are stark. The lo ss of competitiveness is
costing us markets, costing us jobs, and losing us many major employers.
5144 General Debate 12 Sep 2012
So the time for prevarication and passivi ty over the Reserve Bank is over. The
damage needs to be stopped before more irreparable harm is done to our economic
capacity. The bill that New Zealand First has introduced to amend the Reserve Bank of
New Zealand Act will mean the Reserve Ba nk can pursue a bala nced macroeconomic
policy in which price stability, although remaining important, is no longer the
overriding policy objective. We will have an  amended Reserve Bank that is fit for
purpose and will promote growth, jobs, and, mo re important, exports. So, in summary,
everyone agrees the dollar is overvalued—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: No! What should the value be, Andrew?

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Everyone agrees the dollar is  overvalued—the Minister of
Finance said as much this week. The dama ge to our economy is now widespread and
growing. We are undermining our economic ca pacity in the country day by day. The
Government is stuck in passive mode.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: What a shocker of a day
it has been for Labour. You know, Labour had a great chance this afternoon for their
leader to get up and make a real impact in  this House, and what  did he do? The one
question he had, he withdrew. I think ther e would have been major disappointment
amongst the grassroots Labour Party membersh ip out there to see the Labour caucus
performance in question time today. I tell you what, if it is not time for a change of
Labour leadership, there never will be. My advi ce to people over there is that they have
got to grasp the nettle and get on with the tough decisions.
It has not been a good day for Labour online either, because we had Mr Shearer’s
online chat today. I am sure that Labour  supporters, that dwindling number throughout
New Zealand, would have been looking for some real substance. Well, there it was.

items.speaker: Clint asked Mr Shearer
items.text: “How do you get Ne w Zealand out of debt without selling
assets, raising tax, or taking away the few benefits that middle-class New Zealanders
receive?”. Mr Shearer said: “We need to grow the economy, and th at needs pro-growth
tax reform.” And then Sally asked: “Well, what do you mean by pro-growth tax reform,
Mr Shearer?”. Mr Shearer said: “The big chan ge we would make is a capital gains tax.”
So that is the answer. On the one hand, if Labour is in Government with New Zealand
First, we are going to have the exchange rate  fixed, and then the bi g answer is going to
be capital gains. Well, I can tell one that is not going to be what gets New Zealand
going ahead.
What is going to get the country going is sound economic management and the sort
of leadership that John Key is bringing to the country. If you look at that online poll—I
am sure the Labour Party will have  seen it today—1,800 readers of the New Zealand
Herald were asked who they would be voting for: 49 percent National, 22 percent
Labour. They are on course for an absolute shocker. So when we see the sorts of
theatrics we are getting from  Trevor Mallard and co. in  the House today, you can tell
that those people over there have lost the plot.
Meanwhile, what we are focusing on is solid performance in the economy. Unlike
Labour, who were supporting the crazy Gree n bill banning the sale of all land to
overseas owners, a bill that would have rea lly severely dented our economy and sent
terrible signals overseas, unlike them we are getting on and encouraging investment into
New Zealand and making sure we have got th e capital in this country to grow the
economy. A good example, if the Labour Party had been in charge, is that none of these
decisions would have been made. So you would not have had the Japanese investor who
fronted up with the capital to save 60 jobs at Terrace Downs estate in Christchurch. No,
the Labour Party opposed that. You would not have had the American non-profit
organisation that purchased 15 hectares in Richmond and has produced jobs in
construction and tourism, and made sure that  the people working th ere have maintained
12 Sep 2012 General Debate 5145
their jobs. No, that would have been gone under Labour, because it supported that
ridiculous Green bill that would have banned the sale of land to all foreigners. Carbon
Conscious Holdings and Kingheim Ltd would not have been allowed to purchase their
forestry investments, which have produced  jobs and growth in New Zealand. There
would not be any jobs from expansions in new projects by TAG Oil and Bathurst
Resources. They would all be gone under Labo ur. Basically, when you look at it, what
you are hearing from Labour members is just  rhetoric. They are opposed to anything
that results in economic growth. I challenge them—and I hope it is Mr Shearer who gets
up next—to actually say what the Labour Party would do to grow the economy.
Today Mr Shearer was asked some very stra ight questions during his online chat. He
was asked what his stance was on decriminalis ation of cannabis: “David, yes or no; are
you for the decriminalisation of cannabis?”.  “I’m not making policy on the hoof.”, said
Mr Shearer. Mr Shearer could not even say whether he was against our young people
being able to smoke marijuana or not. Well,  I can tell you, on this si de of the House we
are pretty clear-cut on that stuff. I oppose the decriminalisation of marijuana because we
know what it does to our young people. Labour is now trying to deflate the argument
and move it off the agenda.
But what I can say is that the Labour Party is opposed to anything that means jobs or
growth for New Zealanders, and New Zealanders know that. New Zealanders know that
the path ahead is the very sensible course  that John Key has got this Government on. I
think the argument is pretty clear-cut. I thi nk it is being reflected at the polls. The path
ahead is the sensible investment decisions that this Government is encouraging. What
we are seeing from those members is support of policies that are going to lead this
country down the gurgler. The case rests.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I just want to say thank you and
pass on my gratitude to the last speaker, Jonathan Coleman, for helping me to get
elected into the Mt Albert seat. His ongoing a nd persistent efforts were certainly missed
in the last election, but I certainly did appreciate those during the by-election.
Today we have been confronted with a $78 billion figure from the Minister for
Social Development. Nobody quite knows exactly  what that means. It is a meaningless
figure. The last figure that we heard along those lines was fr om the Ministry of Social
Development. It was a $45 billion figure, and nobody quite  knew what that meant,
either. What her figure is s upposed to say, or what she is  claiming it is saying, is the
cost of our social welfare spend in this country.
What this Government is really good at doi ng is measuring not very much and doing
very, very little. So we act ually do not know how we ar e going to move past those
numbers to actual real improvement. But le t me give you some other numbers. These
are the costs to this country of kids growing up in poverty. It  is $8.8 billion a year. That
$8.8 billion a year is what it is costing this country because of kids growing up in
poverty: lost productivity, $2 billion; crime, $2.2 billion; health costs, between $3
billion and $4.5 billion; and social welfare, $1.4 billion. That is $400 billion over a
lifetime. That is nearly 10 times what that Mi nister was talking about in terms of social
welfare. If she actually solved the real pr oblems in this country—the real problem is
about child poverty.
This week we put on the table some proac tive, positive steps forward in terms of
changing the way that we do something abou t the choices that kids have in their
schools. You go to schools across this count ry and you look at those kids at those
schools. They look up at you, and they are ea ger. They are ready to learn and are
willing. Then you look a little bit harder and you notice that many of them do not have
shoes. They have got no jumpers on. They are cold, and many of them, according to
their teachers, come to school without lunche s. We can argue about whether that is the
5146 General Debate 12 Sep 2012
parents’ responsibility or not—of  course it is the parents’ re sponsibility for the kids to
come along to school well fed and with lunch, but  the reality is that they are not. More
than 80,000 kids are coming to school without those things. Without lunch and without
having something to eat before school, of course they are not going to do well in the
classroom—either for themselves or as a distraction to others.
We are proposing to put food into schools to en sure that those kids get the best start.
What does that mean? What does that actually  mean? That means that when those kids
get a good start they do not come out the other end and fall into the unemployment
queue or form part of our health statistics or our crime statistics.
What else are we proposing to do? Actu ally, what we are proposing to do is
something that we only just discovered that Bill English was proposing just a few years
ago, and that is to make sure that every kid has access to Reading Recovery. One in five
children in this country has problems with reading. Reading Recovery has an 80 percent
success rate—80 percent. It is the gold st andard across the world. Yet Reading
Recovery is not available in every one of our schools.
So what we are proposing is making sure that every kid has access to Reading
Recovery, making sure kids have food in their stomachs when they go to school, and
making sure that they get picked up if th ey are having reading di fficulties. This will
mean that they come out the other end and contribute to our  society, and the
meaningless statistics that the social deve lopment Minister came up with today will not
need to be pandered around this Parliament. They are ridiculous. They are ridiculous,
because all they do is throw out a number, when what we  are really looking for is
solutions. This Government has no solutions . If it did have solutions, it would have
come up with them, and we would not be in this situation.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Does it not speak volumes about the
level of confidence in the leadership of the Labour Party that there is fewer than half the
caucus here this afternoon to listen to their leader? I re member in the days when
National was in Opposition, and John Key wa s the leader, that you would have had
every single member of the National caucus down here, backing the leadership and the
team. But having heard the content, I am not surprised that the Labour caucus is sitting
up in their offices embarrassed by the conten t. You see, the Lead er of the Opposition
has just said he does not understand the significance of a $78 billion social welfare
liability. Well, I say to the Leader of the Opposition that until he understands the scale
of the welfare challenge, and the importa nce of getting families into work and off
welfare, he has no prospects of being a Minister—let al one a Prime Minister—in the
Government of New Zealand.
What a contrast there has been over the adjournment in the approaches to the
challenges that face New Zealand. I want to commend Paula Bennett on the powerful
work that she is doing to change this country  for the better, in the way in which she is
dealing with those welfare challenges. You see, Paula Bennett and this John Key - led
Government understand the obligations and responsibilities that must sit alongside
rights. For instance, we on this side of the H ouse say that a person should be able to be
drug tested whether they are in work or whet her they want to get a welfare benefit. The
Leader of the Opposition does not even know where he stan ds on the issue of whether
we should liberalise cannabis laws in this  country. We on this side of the House know
that children need to get access to doctors,  to early childhood education, and to schools
to be able to get ahead in life. That  is why the Minister  has announced a pre-
requirement for those families that we are financing to make sure they meet that
obligation. I hear New Zealanders from Kaitāia to Bluff saying hear, hear!
You know, the biggest absence in commentary from the Labour Party is where they
stand on national standards. Is it not interest ing to see Julia Gillard, the Prime Minister
12 Sep 2012 General Debate 5147
of Australia, championing the cause, and the importance, of measuring how kids do in
Australia, and yet we have a Labour Party in  New Zealand that is so beholden to the
teachers unions that it is not prepared to stand up for what is right and for measuring
how our kids do at school?
But the contrast goes far deeper than that —far deeper than that. You see, what we
heard from the Government over the adjour nment was how we grow the economy, and
from the Opposition we heard how we spend, how we borrow, and how we get New
Zealand further into difficulty. What we ha ve from Labour in that confused and
muddled speech from the Leader of the O pposition is not one mention of the biggest
issue that confronts our country, and that is how we ar e going to grow wages and grow
jobs so that this country can  provide the education, the he alth, and the opportunities for
the next generation of New Zealanders.
So often we on this side of the House have said that Labour is living on some
different planet, and that was reinforced in the contribution today. All around the world
countries are trying to confront  the issues of debt, of defi cits, and of how to grow the
economy. Yet we have not had a single idea from members opposite on how to achieve
those things. Let me just reflect, just quickly, on the good things that this Government is
doing in that space. Firstly, let us look at the issue of jobs. There have been 40,000 new
net jobs created in the last 2 years in th e New Zealand economy, a faster rate of job
growth than any other OECD country, an d it has been achieved in incredibly
challenging financial times.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: What rubbish!

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I ask the member who is interjecting what the
unemployment level is in Spain. It is 24 perc ent. What is it in  Italy and Ireland, and
other countries in Europe? It is in double digits. New Zealand has one of the lowest
levels of unemployment because of the competent economic management, the focus on
growth, and the package of measures that colleagues are rolling out, which gives this
country hope for a brighter future.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: It has not escaped anybody’s attention
that Bill English refused to back the Prim e Minister today, and refused to defend the
Prime Minister’s comments on Reading Rec overy. He would not go  anywhere near it.
When a question was put to the Acting Prime Mi nister he went out of his way to get it
off his desk, because he did not want to b ack the Prime Minister on Reading Recovery.
Why did he not want to do that? Because the comments and the commitments that the
Labour Party has made with re gard to Reading Recovery are the same sentiments that
Bill English was expressing when he wa s in Opposition. And has National done it?
After 4 years, has it delivered on it? No, it has not.
In fact, the problem has got worse. There are fewer decile 1, 2, and 3 schools
delivering Reading Recovery today than th ere were when Bill English was lamenting
the fact that not enough schools were deliver ing it. It is no wonder Bill English was
ducking for cover and was refusing to back John Key on Reading Recovery, because it
would simply have shown once again that wh at Bill English said in Opposition is not
what he has been doing in Government. Noth ing that the National Party said when it
was in Opposition can be relied upon as a guide for what it has been doing in
Government. For 4 years New Zealanders have  been waiting for the brighter future the
National Party promised them, and they are still going to be waiting at the next election,
when they turf National out and introduce a Labour Government, because then they will
actually see the brighter future that New Zealanders hunger for and want to see.
New Zealanders know that edu cation is a core pa rt, a core way that  we can deliver
the brighter future, and it is not going to come from this National Government. This
National Government is destroying the mo st positive aspects of our New Zealand
5148 General Debate 12 Sep 2012
education system, which is one of the best in the world. National is tinkering with it,
experimenting with it, and turning our kids into guinea pigs. It is turning to the countries
in the world that are way down the ladder a nd have a worse education system than us
and it is copying the things they do. It is copying the things they do, and it is hoping that
that is going to improve our education system. Well, it will not.
The National Party tells parents that they cannot trust teachers. The National Party, at
its core, hates teachers. They really do not like teachers over there in the National Party,
and they keep telling parents they cannot tr ust teachers. Their solution to improving the
quality of teaching was to make classes bigger,  and when that failed they resorted to a
new plan to introduce charter schools wit hout having qualified teachers in them. That
was National’s solution to the fact that pa rents overwhelmingly rejected its plan for
bigger class sizes. So what did National memb ers do? They went back to the drawing
board and said: “Let’s just not have qualifie d teachers. Let’s just reduce the number of
qualified teachers in charter schools.” That is not going to be the solution to the
problem. We have a very efficient educati on system when it comes to building schools.
What is the National Party’s solution to th at? “Oh,” National says , “we better get the
for-profit private sector involved. We are going to build some public-private partnership
schools that cost more than the regular pub lic schools are going to cost.” That is the
bright future the National Party is promising to New Zealanders.
We should know, of course, that National is not committed to qualified teachers,
because one of the very first things it did was to lower the standards for early childhood
education by reducing the number of qualified teachers that an early childhood
education centre is expected to have.

items.speaker: Katrina Shanks
items.text: That’s rubbish.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: That was one of the first things Anne Tolley did when she
became the Minister of Education, and I ag ree with Katrina Sha nks—it was a rubbish
decision that Anne Tolley made when she lowered the standards for early childhood
education.
This is a Government that does not have a clear agenda for education. It does not
have any idea what it is trying to achieve . It has the charter schools idea—the silver
bullet. So now we are going to have the “Mer rill Lynch School for Ethical Investment”.
We are going to have the “KFC School for Nutritional Studies”. We will have the
“Monsanto School of Organi c Agriculture”, a nd the “Rothmans School for Health
Studies”. That is fundamentally what the National Party believes—that running schools
is a business that someone should be able to  make a profit out of, and they do not even
have to deliver on quality. They do not ev en have to deliver on quality. It does not
matter whether they have qualified teachers in the classrooms of these new charter
schools. That does not matter to the Nationa l Party, because, fundamentally, it does not
know what it is trying to achie ve in education. It does not have a programme that will
improve our education system.
What we need to be focused on is how we  go from having one of the best education
systems in the world to having the best educat ion system in the world. That is what the
Labour Party under David Shearer’s leadership is committed to. That is what we are
going to deliver when we win the next general election.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: One of the really difficult things the public
has to do at the moment is to try to discer n what Labour actually stands for. Dr Nick
Smith has gone through some very excellent exam ples of that in the realm of education.
I want to touch on this in relation to fi scal policy, because there was a fascinating
exchange during question time today when the Deputy Prime Minister, in suggesting
that Opposition parties advocat e an exchange rate that was 20 percent or so lower,
received a barrage of interjection from Mr Mallard and Mr Goff. In fact, Mr Mallard
12 Sep 2012 General Debate 5149
even received a withering look from the Sp eaker as he said something like “Don’t tell
lies.”
I am actually very interested  in this, because I know that Mr Parker has just been
overseas and has been blogging about his trip to the US and the UK. He was meeting
with some of the world’s greatest economists, apparently not to listen very carefully and
learn as much as he could but to discuss his ideas on monetary policy and the exchange
rate—not to listen and learn but to tell the best economists in the world what he thought.

items.speaker: He says in the blog
items.text: “He agreed”—quoting Mr Olivier Blanchard, so he obviously was
saying that he agreed with Mr Parker—“countries need to attend to the competitiveness
of their exchange rates.” I can only infer from  that that Labour and Mr Parker at least
want lower exchange rates.
More extraordinarily, there is a belief, which I believe is Mr Parker’s, that exchange
rates can be controlled for l onger periods than have traditionally been acknowledged by
most economists—here it is—“w ithout losing the bat tle to control inflation.” So I want
members to consider what a 20 percent lower exchange rate would mean for consumers.
Do members know those $2 a litre petrol prices? They would go to $2.80, without any
other inflationary impacts. Petrol would go straight to $2.80. What would that mean for
transport? Well, a lot of our freight goods are transported by road, by trucks. That is the
cost of goods, even those we export. So our exports become less competitive, even
though the exchange rate is lower. In te rms of imported goods—often those that form
the basis of the products that we value-add and then export agai n—they will be 20
percent to 25 percent more expensive. The cost of home appliances, all our imported
electrical goods, will be 20 percent to 25 percent higher. In an inflationary environment,
lowering the exchange rate will only add to inflation.
I worked for a bank in the 1980s, when I was giving out mortgages of 19.5 percent
and 20.5 percent—runaway infl ation. Nobody can remember what the exchange rate
was then—nobody can remember what the excha nge rate was—but they sure as heck
know what their mortgage rates were. We ar e now paying mortgage rates of, what, 5.75
percent to 5.8 percent floating rates. I thi nk the public of New Z ealand are entitled to
know the impact of Labour’s proposal—eve n if it was possible—to lever down the
exchange rate. How on earth it  would do that without taking  one of the biggest fiscal
crapshoots in world economic history is ab solutely beyond me. But the public need to
know what that will mean for their income s, and for the cost of living in their
households, and I can tell you it is extraordinarily high.
The impact on that in jobs is anybody’s guess, but one of the things that I do know is
that Labour members are very good at telling half a story well. This is a Government
that is firmly focused on jobs and growth. Yes, there is concern when things like the
Kawerau pulp and paper mill and the T īwai Point aluminium smelter announce plans to
reduce hundreds of jobs. T īwai is fascinating. Mr Parker, in the previous Parliament,
decried the fact that it was ge tting what he described as 90  percent subsidies. In fact,
when we softened Labour’s emissions trading scheme, the subsidy, if you want to call it
that, went from 80 percent to 90 percent. La bour members were quite happy to do it
when they were in Government. That lower exchange rate might increase the value of
aluminium exports—that is not clear—but it would certainly increase the costs of
production.
So, yes, it is concerning when those jobs go, but let us talk about the growth in jobs
as well. Let us talk abou t IBM and Unitec announcing 400 jobs; Todd Corporation and
Methanex adding another 500 construction jobs for methanol manufacturing at
Motunui; The Hobbit—we do not need to talk too much about The Hobbit— and
Bathurst Resources, a salve on the West Coast, which is experiencing some very
challenging times with Solid Energy jobs at ri sk. Bathurst is quietly getting on, growing
5150 General Debate 12 Sep 2012
jobs, growing exports, and doing well for Ne w Zealanders. The news  is very good. It
would be bad if we tried to engineer our exchange rate down.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe. It is Conservation W eek this week, and it is
particularly significant this year because of the hist oric announcement that Ng āi Tūhoe
are prepared to accept the Crown’s offer to settle their claims and grievances under the
Treaty of Waitangi. A major part of that settlement relates to Te Urewera National Park.
The Government plans to introduce special legi slation that would gi ve the park its own
separate legal identity, rather than bei ng a national park managed under the National
Parks Act 1980. That will be landmark legisla tion because of the way in which it must
combine both biodiversity protectio n and adequate recognition of T ūhoe’s cultural,
spiritual, and historical connection with Te Urewera, and we look forward to it.
But the Minister of Conservation has ma rked Conservation Week by announcing an
increase in penalties for the smuggling of our native wildlife. That is very welcome, but
getting tougher on wildlife smugglers cannot disguise this Government’s neglect of the
spectacular landscapes and of our native, indigenous wildlife a nd plant communities.
The previous speaker, Michael Woodhouse, wa s a case in point. He was talking about
Bathurst Resources quietly gett ing on with the job. He was totally failing to appreciate
the significance of the Denniston Plateau wher e that open-cast coalmine by this Aussie
coalminer is proposed to take place. The De nniston Plateau is one of the key areas of
conservation land that this Government should be protecting and preserving. It is one of
our special places. It is no place for an open-cast coalmine.
This Government repeatedly talks about balance. If it was serious about balance, then
it would recognise that the St ockton Plateau has been much  mined over recent decades
and much of the remainder of the Stockton Plateau, which is adjacent to the Denniston
Plateau, is proposed for mining, and it would keep the Denniston Plateau and the unique
coal measure ecosystems, which that plateau is home to, as cons ervation land that is
protected because of its distinctive charact er. These coal measure ecosystems, their
plants and animals, are adapted to live in  these very harsh grow ing conditions in the
infertile, acidic soils. We have got over 20 different species of earthworm on the plateau
alone. That is more than exist on the rest  of the West Coast. We have got giant
carnivorous Powelliphanta land snails, which go right back  to Gondwana. We have got
a giant weta species. We have got species that were previously undiscovered, like a
moth species, until the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society’s bioblitz.
The Denniston Plateau is no place fo r this Government’s crazy, economic
development, trash-the-environment plans. It  is a place that should be protected as
conservation land. It has got small, pygmy plants. The Gove rnment fails to recognise
that these species have value. It is miserly when it comes to investing in conservation. It
has cut $54 million from the conservation budget,  yet it is spendthrift when it comes to
propping up polluters like Fonterra sharehol ders and like coalminers by subsidising
them through the very flawed emissions tr ading scheme. Yet it slashes money from
conservation, and it fails to recognise that our public protected lands are the essential
infrastructure of our economy and that a h ealthy environment is the basis for a healthy
economy.
The Government needs to invest much more in conservation, not the piddling
expenditure that we have seen  on Conservation Week this week. It is a reflection, I
guess, of the overall miserliness with th e conservation budget that this year the
department has spent $3,000 on Conservation Week. It used to spend $30,000 each year
on Conservation Week, enabling it to educat e a lot of children, provide literature,
handbooks, posters, bookmarks, and to have a lot more activity around New Zealand in
reaching out and showing a lot of schoolchildr en how special a lot of our conservation
lands are and why we have to protect our fo rests, our wetlands, and our estuaries. That
12 Sep 2012 General Debate 5151
has been cut back as part of an overall cu tback in conservation funding, which is seeing
failure to do adequate pest control, failure to acquire new unprotected areas to add to the
conservation estate, and failure to do pr oper advocacy—the depart ment being absent
from a number of critical resource manageme nt hearings. Yet, instead, the Government
is propping up polluters through the failed and flawed emissions trading scheme.
A healthy environment is the basis of a healthy economy. Protecting places like the
Denniston Plateau, not opening them up to mi ning, is protecting those areas for present
and future generations for their values and their value for tourism.

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call in the general
debate. I want to touch on job creation and employment, because that is what this
Government is focused on. It is focused on getting more jobs, creating good-quality
jobs, and growing our economy. Let me put so me facts on the tabl e to begin with. I
want to talk about our unemployment ra te: 6.7 percent is our unemployment rate.
Obviously, it is higher than what we want it to  be, but it is what it is right here and right
now. When you compare it with other countr ies around the world, we are certainly in a
really good position. There are many countries th at are envious of what we have done
with our employment. Unemployment in Sp ain is 24 percent. Youth unemployment in
Spain is 51 percent.
Let us look at Europe. There is 11 per cent across-the-board unemployment. Greece
has 22 percent. France, Italy, Ireland, Turkey, and Poland, to name just a few, are all in
double digits. Britain and the USA have 8.3 percent. Canada has 7.3 percent. So New
Zealand is doing really well compared with th e rest of the world, and that is what we
should focus on.
Let me put some more facts on the table.  This Government has created 60,000 more
jobs in the last 2 years—60,000 more jobs—a nd we are going to create another 154,000
over the next 4 years. A significant number of those will be in Christchurch, with the
rebuild of Christchurch.
This is a really interesting fact I want to talk about: more people are employed as a
percentage of the population on this side of the Tasman than in Australia. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Ther e are just over 49,000 people
on the unemployment benefit, which is 18,00 0 fewer than 18 months ago. That is a
significant change when you think where Ne w Zealand has been, what the financial
crisis has looked like, and where we are goi ng now. We want to create more jobs in
New Zealand. We want to do it through being competitive. We want to do it to ensure
that our companies are productive and that our businesses can invest, grow, employ, and
pay higher wages in New Zealand. So that is what we are focusing on—our
businesses—because unless we can create th at growth in New Zealand, we are not
going to create more jobs.
We have some fantastic companies in New Zealand that are growing, going into new
markets, and doing it all on their own. This Government has provided a framework for
them to be able to grow and develop, a nd they are going out and doing it on their own.
A perfect example is in the Hutt—I am sure the member Chris Hipkins has been to see
it—and that is Fraser Engineering. It is an absolutely fantastic, progressive company in
New Zealand. It produces fire engines. Not only does it produce all the fire engines in
New Zealand but it has now entered the Australian market and is producing fire engines
in Australia as well. It is a very progressive company that is doing great work, and it has
been very innovative, investing a lot of its money back into its research to ensure that it
stays cutting edge.
This Government is creating a lot of initiati ves to ensure that we  have got jobs. One
of the big initiatives has been the 90-day trial period. This is allowing employers and
5152 General Debate 12 Sep 2012
employees to work together to ensure that  businesses can employ more people, because
what we have had are businesses not being prepared to take a bit of risk. So with the 90-
day trial period, it has allowed businesses to take a bit of a risk to employ somebody
they might not have employed, or somebody whom they were unsure whether there was
a position for or not, and put them on a 90- day trial period to see whether it would
work. It has been extremely successful in New Zealand. In  fact, the Department of
Labour has done some research around this. Eighty percent of those people who went
through the 90-day trial period have been em ployed. Employers said that they would
not have hired to begin with—40 percent of employers said that they would not have
hired to begin with—unless they had that 90-d ay trial period. This initiative has created
13,000 more jobs in New Zealand. That is significant—13,000 jobs from one policy. It
is one policy that has created jobs in New Zealand, which has been fantastic.
We also know that to do that we have to support our businesses and give them the
support they need to be able to grow. You would not be a National member of
Parliament for Wellington—

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: That last speech by Katrina Shanks was an example of
just how much the National Government lack s in ambition for this country. Apparently,
we are supposed to feel that it is doing a good job because the unemployment rate is not
at 24 percent. That is what we are told. We are supposed to be tha nkful and grateful to
that Government because we are not at 24 percent unemployment. Well, when Labour
was the Government, it boasted the lowest  unemployment rate in the OECD—not just
saying: “Well, gosh, you know, Spain and Portugal and Ireland ar e ahead of us, and
Greece is ahead of us.” Actually, unemploy ment was the lowest in the OECD under
Labour. That is because we actually had a plan and we knew what we were doing.
If you want to look for vision these days on the political scene in New Zealand, then
you need to look no further than David Sh earer’s speech on education. He was not
prepared to sit back and say: “Well, as long as we’re just a little bit below Spain and
Portugal and Ireland and Greece, we’re fine.” He was not prepared to say that. What
David Shearer said was that Labour will ensu re the world’s best education—the best
education in the world—is available at ev ery school. We want ev ery child and every
community to have access to world-class education. We are not satisfied with the
situation where parents have to  drive often past four or fi ve school gates to get to a
school that they feel is the right one for their child. We do not agree with this idea of
charter schools, of actually giving public m oney over to the private sector to make a
profit out of education.
In fact, what David Shearer said—he wa s the one coming up with the fresh new
ideas—was: “We’re going to actually deal with  the real issues there in the community.
We’re going to work with community agencies to put food in low-decile schools.”—the
very thing that the National Government is in complete denial over. Labour knows what
is going on out in the community and we ha ve a plan to fix it. We will also extend
Reading Recovery to all schools, because we just cannot afford to have kids dropping
out without basic skills. We are also goi ng to introduce clear and easy-to-understand
school report cards to parents so they know what is going on in their schools. The
Education Review Office produces reports now, but for most parents it is actually like
reading gobbledegook. I think it is going to be great for parents to get an easy-to-
understand report on how their school is actu ally doing. Those are the commitments
from Labour and that is where a vision is coming from on the political scene in New
Zealand at the moment.
Contrast that with the Nati onal Party. What has it got to say about education? Well,
the only plans it has for education are to in crease class sizes so that teachers have many
more children to try to interact with, and, of course, we all know , and all the parents
12 Sep 2012 General Debate 5153
throughout this country know, that the quali ty of education will go down. Well, what
are its other plans? Charter schools, as I said before, without qualified teachers. It wants
to dumb down the quality of teaching by intr oducing charter schools. That is the vision
that the National Government has, and league tables. T oday we learn about possible
exams for 3 and 4-year-olds. That is where it is heading next. That is where it is heading
next, because Hekia Parata had plenty of opportunity in question time today to deny that
she was going down that path. She absolutely  would not deny that work is being done
on introducing national standards for our pr eschool children. Thre e and 4-year-olds
being under exam pressure is not the vision for New Zealand. It is  not the vision that
Labour has.
But it is not only with regard to the threat  of exams for 3 and 4-year-olds that the
National Government is in trouble with  early childhood education. Yesterday the
Minister for Social Development, Paula Bennett, was actually  announcing a whole
series of compulsions, but compulsions only for the children of beneficiaries, to have to
take part in early childhood e ducation, at ages 3 and 4. But here is the strange thing:
costs for early childhood education under this Government have risen four times the rate
of wages since 2010. This Government ha s been busily putting fees up in early
childhood education, and now it is going to punish beneficiaries because they cannot
afford to send their children to early childhood education. It is going to punish not only
the beneficiaries but the child ren of those beneficiaries because they cannot afford to
send their children to early childhood education.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to take the
opportunity to speak in the general debate today, to comment on the fantastic progress
this Government is making with  things that really matter to New Zealand. It is making
great progress with th e building of an economic platform  that will set this country on
the way to a brighter future.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Has the member learnt how to do supplementary questions
yet?

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I would remind the member that I am talking, not him.
I wanted to just comment on comments th at we have heard this afternoon about
education from the Labour Party, which clear ly has forgotten that it has been only 4
years since it had an opportuni ty to sort out our educatio n policy. It did absolutely
nothing about it, and the reason we have had to  increase the expenditure in education in
the last 4 years is because of the neglect it suffered in the previous 9 years.
I want to also, while I am on the topic of  education, just make a couple of comments
on some stuff that Mr Hipkins talked a bout in respect of education, and wonder
seriously whether he ever visits a school, because, frankly, I do not think he does. In my
electorate we also have, inte restingly, decile 1 schools. We have all ranges of schools.
In those communities they find ways of ensuring that children go to school with shoes
on, and they find ways of ensuring that ch ildren have uniforms on and that they are
provided with food during school hours, whethe r or not their parents can achieve that. I
think that that is the great strength we s ee in our school system today. We have some
amazing school teachers, they provide a w onderful service for our community, and I
think that for the Labour Party members to be speaking in the way they have been about
teachers and education in the last half an hour is extraordinarily stupid.
In the 8 months I have been privileged to represent the Rangit īkei electorate in this
Parliament, I have seen and heard many  exciting and forward-thinking people who
comment on the way the New Zealand economy is moving in what can only be seen as
extremely difficult times. We have a Minister  for Social Development who is driving,
and understands, the need to reform our welfar e environment, to both encourage people
5154 General Debate 12 Sep 2012
into work and get an education that enables them to work productively for New Zealand
and their own futures.
We have a welfare system that cares for our elderly. In rural New Zealand that is
pretty important, because we have the privilege in New Zealand of being able to be born
and die in our communities. I think it is most important that we can live our life in one
community.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Unless you’re forced to move to Australia by this Government.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: The other thing that happens in electorates like mine—which
may well be foreign to Christchurch—is that  because of the extraordinarily testing
amount of manual work that people in the Rangit īkei electorate do, the retirement age
suits those people, and we need to protect th eir ability to retire and get some years of
comfortable retirement as a result of our current retirement age.
We also have a Minister of Education fully occupied in increasing the skills,
knowledge, and achievement of our school-leav ers. As I have already commented, I
think our education system is on the right tr ack, and in my electorate the teachers are
reasonably comfortable with the way we are moving forward. To complete the triangle,
we have the Minister of Health driving a very strong performance in our health business
in New Zealand, in very challenging times. Our expectations and survival rates are
increasing dramatically and adding challenges to the health sector at an unprecedented
rate.
These three sectors are like a tripod. They keep our economy based, and they give us
a base from which to leverage from. Having set that platform, I want to turn to the
productive sector. This is, of course, what the Rangit īkei does best. We grow trees, we
grow sheep, we grow cattle, we produce milk, we grow root vegetables, and we service
agriculture the world over. We service ag riculture not only th rough our science and
development, which take pla ce at Massey University, but al so through some innovative
businesses that are growing the New Zealand economy.
I want to just talk very briefly about three issues th at have an impact on New
Zealand’s economy, and particularly on the Rangit īkei electorate, which relies heavily
on tourism and agriculture for its living.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: No tourist wants to go to Palmerston North.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I must remind you that the member  of Parliament for Palmerston
North sits on the other side of the House. I want to talk very briefly about the emissions
trading scheme and capital gains tax, and the effect they would have on an electorate
like mine and its potential to produce jobs and to fix the environment in the current
system we live in. Our environment is pa rticularly precious to both tourism and
agriculture, and if we do not invest in the fu ture and fix some of the challenges we have
around our environment, we are going to have serious problems in the future.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take the last call in
this general debate. We have had to sit here  for the last hour and endure the National
Party members opposite chanting that they ar e on the right track wi th job creation and
employment, and that they are creating their ve rsion of a brighter fu ture. This has been
hollow rhetoric from hollow members. What we have is aspiration that today we are not
Spain, and that we do not have unemployment of 24 percent. Well, we on this side of
the House want something more for our nati on. We want something more for our future
than that. We want something more th an the 160,000 people whom members opposite
have thrown on the scrap h eap of unemployment. We do not want to see 50,000 people
leaving every year for Australia because there is no future here for them.
How does Labour propose to do this? Well, La bour sees education as an investment
in our future and not a cost to cut, which is what members opposite have shown.
Education is at the very f oundation of a fairer and more prosperous New Zealand. We
12 Sep 2012 General Debate 5155
have heard from members opposite that we have  to get the economy right if we want to
pay for health and education. Well, we w ill never get the economy right if we do not
invest in our future and our education system . It is not an either /or situation. A good
education provides our children with a lifetime of opportunities. Children have the right
to the best education from their first day of  school through to their first day on the job.
Labour has a vision for education. It is a priority for Labour. What we have is a
National Government that is presiding over a disaster in education.
Today I want to focus on three areas of th is disaster. I want to talk about the
University of Canterbury, where today the library went into lockdown because there
was the first of what I predict will be many student protests. I want to point out that this
was quite a small student protest today.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Not like the ones that member was part of.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It was not like the ones this  member was part of. It was
because there is a Government opposite that  has failed the University of Canterbury.
Post-earthquake, like so many things in Ca nterbury and Christchurch, the Government
made a commitment to support the Universi ty of Canterbury. Bu t are we seeing
support? No. We are seeing one in five staf f at the university lose their job. We are
seeing an 18 percent reduction in that workfo rce. We are seeing a Government that is
doing nothing but failing the university.
If the Government’s own scenarios of ec onomic recovery are to be believed, the
rebuild will be under way, student  numbers will recover, and th e university has to be at
the heart of that rebuild. But we see a Government that puts no confidence in the
university, and is simply failing it. Instead, the Government is resorting to bullying
tactics with the university, w ith its own internal papers s howing and telling us that the
implicit message from the Tertiary Education Commission and the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment is that if the institution is willing to lead the way
with cuts that could easily run to hundreds of jobs, the State may invest in the
university. The university thinks that this is reprehensible. What we have are students
being the collateral damage of this—students who are gi ving up on their university and
do not see their future residing there.
Just as I was reading the Twitter reports of the mini-protest at the University of
Canterbury today, I received an invitation to an event. It is  a collaboration between the
Canterbury Museum and the University of Ca nterbury called Canterbury Tales. It is
going to show artefacts from the university and the museum. Well, you know what? My
fear is that graduates and students from th e University of Canterbury will soon be the
only artefact. This is a university that is in trouble, and this is a university that this
Government needs to step up and do something about.
The second disaster of edu cation in Canterbury that I want to talk about is the
Canterbury schools blueprint that  is going to be released tomorrow. The Minister of
Education is claiming that it will foster close connections across the education sector.
This is far from the truth. Instead, what we  are seeing today is Christchurch swirling
with rumour, with uncertainty—
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
