Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I thought I would conclude my speech by quoting
from Philip Fierlinger from Xero. He is its h ead of software design. He said: “We have
chosen not to seek software patents because we don’t believe they are good for the
industry. They divert resources and attenti on, both when creating and enforcing. More
importantly, they stifle innovation and restrict competition. Competition is a good thing.
We welcome competition as a motivation to build a better product. We also stand on the
shoulders of giants—our predecessors who designed and invented fundamental software
5176 Patents Bill 12 Sep 2012
mechanisms and patterns that make software what it is today.” That is a New Zealand
innovator. That is the sort of person who w ill be locked out by the giant, international
companies, if the Minister’s Supplementary Order Paper 120 is agreed to.
The Labour members will support the second  reading of the Patents Bill, but we
plead with the National Party members to look at Supplementary Order Paper 123 in the
name of Clare Curran and to support it. I wa nt to make it absolu tely clear that the
Committee stage will take a very long time, beca use we will fight them tooth and nail if
that amendment is not agreed to, and we will not support later stages of this bill if, in
fact, the National Party decides to s upport overseas-owned, giant semi-monopolies—
semi-monopolies—against our local software designers.
Bill read a second time.
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I move, That the
Biosecurity Law Reform Bill  be now read a third time . The Biosecurity Law Reform
Bill makes a wide range of improvements to the legislation that underpins our
biosecurity system. The initial policy devel opment work was started under the previous
Labour Government, and I want to acknowle dge the continued s upport of the Labour
Party. The bill was introduced during the last Parliament in November 2010, and was
considered by the Primary Production Committ ee in the first half of 2011. The bill was
reported back to the committee in June 2011, and was read a second time before
Parliament was dissolved for the general election.
I talked in my first read ing speech about th e key themes that run across the
amendments of the bill, and it is useful to re-emphasise those again. Firstly, we need to
continue to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the biosecurity system. We need
to make sure that resources are allocated acco rding to the level of risk and are used to
deliver the greatest level of protection possibl e. Secondly, we need to ensure that there
is clarity around roles and responsibilities, and to promote partnerships and
collaboration. Protecting New Zealand from biosecurity ri sk cannot be the role of
Government alone. We need to ensure that we harness the combined efforts of others
who are well placed to act, such as industr y and such as regional councils. Thirdly, we
need to futureproof the legislation so that it has the flexibility to allow the biosecurity
system to continue to evolve over time.
The bill adds a number of new provisions that will improve effectiveness and
efficiency in the management of biosecurity risk at our borders. These include improved
powers to gather information and use it for ri sk profiling so as to ensure that the
resources are allocated according to the leve l of risk, adding a new duty that requires
importers to ensure that their goods comply with the applicable import rules, improving
the enforcement options for dealing with non-compliance at the border, and improving
the tools for dealing with the biosecurity risks that are presented by craft.
The bill will help to provide clarity around the roles and responsibilities, and
promote partnerships and collaboration. A key initiative in this area is the Government-
industry agreement for readin ess and response. Over the last 12 months tremendous
progress has been made in this regard. Indus try organisations are working more closely
with the Ministry for Primary Industries on taking this init iative forward. The
Government-industry agreement will promote be tter prioritisation of activities in the
readiness and response area, im prove preparedness for incurs ions, and enable industry
perspectives and expertise to be brought to the decision-making table.
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5177
The bill includes a number of amendments that will futureproof this legislation.
These include allowing for increased us e of electronic systems and enabling the
Biosecurity Act to be used to manage bios ecurity risks that arise in the exclusive
economic zone.
Of the many other enhancements that the bi ll makes, I would li ke to also briefly
mention, firstly, improving the information that is available on the FarmsOnline
database to support incursion responses, and, secondly, impo rtant changes in the pest
management area, including streamlining the process for developing pest management
plans.
Members from across the House have ta lked in previous debates about how
important the biosecurity system is to Ne w Zealand and our economy. I would like to
emphasise to the House that I am in co mplete agreement about the importance of
biosecurity to our country. I would also li ke to acknowledge the genuine concern of
growers, farmers, and producers about New Zealand’s biosecurity system. I encourage
them to raise their concerns with me and to engage in constructive debate, as is their
right. However, I am disappoi nted at the manner in wh ich biosecurity has been
frequently used as a political football by some  politicians and some  industry leaders. I
hope that the passage of this bill with good cross-party support will bring about more
constructive engagement, both in Parliament and outside, rather than the continuation of
some of the negative politics of recent times.
I would like to take this  opportunity to personally thank the staff throughout New
Zealand’s biosecurity system. They are hard-working, they ar e dedicated to doing their
best, and they deserve to be congratulated on their consistently hi gh standard of work,
which has ensured that New Zealand’s biosecurity system is, indeed, world class.
As I have said before, biosecurity is, and always will be, my highest priority as the
Minister for Primary Industries. This bill reflects that by bringing in reforms that will be
of benefit across the whole of the biosecurity system. I commend this bill to the House.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labou r—West Coast - Tasman) : I was very
pleased to hear the Minister for Primary Industries commit once again to the biosecurity
system and the importance of it for our ec onomy. Indeed, I have just come from a
Young Farmers gathering with the Minister here in Wellington. It was a great event,
hosted by the Young Farmers, where the chief executive of the Ministry for Primary
Industries said that biosecurity, as he has said before, is the single most important
consideration, and the single bi ggest threat, to primary in dustries in this country. I
absolutely agree.

items.speaker: Can I quote something
items.text: “I told you so. It  had to happen, and it did. On 8 May the
export of produce from New Zealand worth $2. 5 billion per year was put in doubt when
one male Queensland fruit fly was found in a pheromone trap in Avondale.” These are
not my words; these are from Andrew Fent on, President of Hortic ulture New Zealand.
He said it was only a matter of time, not a ma tter of if. He said that Horticulture New
Zealand has been going on about this for y ears, that cost cut ting kicked in with
restructuring for greater effi ciency and effectiveness, a nd that “we lost 100 percent X-
ray of baggage entering our borders.” The num ber of front-line sta ff and detector dogs
has been reduced in favour of passenger profiling.
We think biosecurity is the single biggest  threat to this country—to our whole
economy. We supported most of the provisions in the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill—in
fact, we initiated them—but we were concer ned that the Government, in pushing ahead
with this bill, at the same time cut funding to  front-line biosecurity in its first Budget,
and has now slashed front-line staff and st aff at Biosecurity New Zealand by about 90
staff. The Minister just got up in the House a nd said that the Government thinks that it
is the most important thing for primary pr oduction. Well, if one fruit fly can put $2.5
5178 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012
billion worth of exports at ris k, think of what one bit of dirt  with foot and mouth on it
on the soles of the shoes of any used or unused footwear coming into this country would
cost this economy. It is in the billions and billions of dollars.
We have agreed to support this bill, b ecause it does bring in  some new provisions
that allow better information-sharing acros s Government agencies. It, however, also
puts in place basically a system of self-re gulation. The National Party has been known
for self-regulation. In fact, it did it in the mining industry, it did it in the building
industry, and it did it in  electricity. In fact, everywhere it has done it, there has been a
disaster. It is doing it also in the area of  the meat industry, where companies will now
self-regulate on meat inspection. There are re al dangers when industries under pressure
cut corners. The component of self-regulati on here—where, in the Minister’s words,
exporters have to share the responsibility—pl aces the whole economy of our country in
the hands of what might be some desperate importers with their backs to the wall, trying
to make a buck to survive. Well, that is simply not good enough. We need a robust,
secure front-line system analysing risk offshor e, analysing risk as the people and all the
imported goods come to this country, and having robust, very secure front-line checking
systems in place—never mind what might happen should an outbreak occur.
That is another component of the bill— Government-industry agreements. Industries
have been very concerned because, in fact, the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries—
as it was, and then it was the Ministry of Agriculture and Forest ry, and now it is the
Ministry for Primary Industries—was dictating to industries what th ey were likely to
incur by way of costs should there be an incursion of the Queensland fruit fly, the
painted apple moth, varroa, or the numbers of  experiences that we have, unfortunately,
had to face, and heaven forbid if we were ever to face a foot-and-mouth outbreak. Costs
now would be shared by industry and by the Government. Some may say that that is
fine, because they are the beneficiaries. The problem is that when importers bring
products into the country or pe ople travel, they actually ar e the ones providing the risk.
They are the ones—they are the exacerbato rs—who are threatening the industries here.
Industry, without the ability to have some say on how that is managed, thought that very
unfair.
The Minister has introduced a Supplement ary Order Paper that does go some way to
addressing industry concerns—that is, it commits to consultation around how incursions
would be managed here, but also some di scussion into how fr ont-line biosecurity
systems are run. With that Supplementary Or der Paper, on balance, the Labour Party is
prepared to support the bill on the basis of improvements made around technology and
upgrading the systems of information gather ing and sharing. But we do not support this
bill on the basis that we are endorsing the current biosecurity systems in this country.
This is one component. It is a modernisation, as the Minister said, in some ways.
I received today NZ Grower , a magazine. It says that the officials and the
Government are determined to impose on the growers of capsicums, cucumbers,
zucchinis, and tomatoes a new import health standard. In spite of our ability to grow all
those things, supermarkets and others want to import those products into this country,
and the Government wants to dumb dow n the import health standards for the
importation of those things. The growers thi nk that places us at greater risk of a
biosecurity incursion. The new import health standards allow—Mr Nick Smith probably
does not know this—a certain number of fruit fly eggs and larvae to enter New Zealand,
because that is an acceptable level of risk  under the proposed import health standards.
That is not good enough. That is an outra geous dumbing down of the biosecurity
protection of this country, to all the growers in that horticultural area. The growers have
an opportunity to submit. I hope the Minister  is listening. He has not been listening on
many things. I hope he listens to them, because in no way are we supporting the
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5179
Government in the dumbing down of import health standards, as I said, for these
horticultural products.
There is currently a legal ba ttle in the courts, because pork producers in this country
have had to go to court to uphold and protect  their industry, and to uphold the standards
that will keep out porcine reproductive a nd respiratory syndrome—basically, the AIDS
of the pork industry. We do not have it. Austra lia does not have it. Virtually every other
country in the world has it, and this Govern ment wants to dumb down the import health
standards to allow the importation of pork that places far greater risk of the transfer of
porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome from Canada or any European country—
or anywhere else in the world, effectively, because they have got it—into our country.
Why would we do that? It is dumb, it is cost cutting, and it is ideology by the
Government over there, which says we should let the market forces determine where we
should lie. The members over ther e are shaking their h eads. Read this. It is saying that
the import health standards for capsicums and tomatoes are proposed to be dumbed
down. We know it is in the ar ea of pork. We are concer ned about importing honey, and
we know that the Government cut front-lin e biosecurity border protection services—
fact. No debate—that is a fact.
The Government and the next speaker might say “Oh, we have good systems and we
have all these things in place.”, but the fact is that we got a Queensland fruit fly through
the border and through the systems. We pi cked it up, thankfully. I am acknowledging
that the systems here can pick that up, hope fully every time. But, I guess, the more
border breaches that occur, the less likely we are to pick up each and every one of them.
In supporting this bill, which allows the modernisation of  parts of th e biosecurity
system, in no way does Labour support th e dumbing down of biosecurity across the
board in this country. It is the one single th ing that keeps the Director-General awake at
night, he said. It is the singl e biggest threat to this economy, because we still rely on
biological production, we still rely on prim ary production, and this Government has not
been prepared to put the resources in to ensure the level of risk is appropriate.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: This Biosecurity Law Reform Bill is
the most substantive change in New Zealand biosecurity laws for more than 15 years. I
want to challenge the member who has just spoken opposite, Damien O’Connor, who
has beaten his chest around how important biosecurity is. Why is it that in the three
terms—9 years—of a Labour Government, we did not have any substantive law reform
in the very area of biosecu rity? Let us just go through the track record of this
Government in biosecurity. In our very fi rst year in Government, National brought in
laws that more than doubled the fines fo r those who breach our biosecurity laws, and
this evening in the House after a comprehensive review of our biosecurity laws we have
this very substantive bill that improves our laws. For all the huff and the puff from
Damien O’Connor, did you not hear the word s “But we’re going to  support the bill.”?
He knows in his heart of hearts that this  is good law that will help protect New
Zealand’s vital exporting industries.
I want to challenge the member on a few aspe cts of his speech. The first is that like
every Labour spokesperson he promises more spending. It does not matter whether it is
education, health, an extra TV channel, puttin g the school age down to 4, or more
money for ACC, every single one of Labour’s spokespeople is hopping around the
country promising more money. And the simple question is that the challenge that faces
every Western Government is where the money is coming from. I have a very specific
question that Damien O’Connor needs to an swer, given that ra ve: how much extra
money per year will Labour commit to biosecurity?
Hon Damien O’Connor: You wait and see.
5180 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Oh, you wait and see! You wa it and see! What sort of
weasel words—what sort of weasel words! I have a copy here of Labour’s biosecurity
policy at the last election. You would have th ought that after all the rhetoric from Mr
O’Connor that Labour would have had some hard  dollars on the table, and that it felt so
strongly that it had a certai n amount of extra money th at it was going to put into
biosecurity. Do you know what? Not one spec ific dollar amount was committed by Mr
O’Connor in respect of biosecurity.
The member Mr O’Connor has said that th e fruit fly incident that occurred in
Avondale shows our biosecurity systems ar e not working. He is wrong. Exactly the
opposite is true—exactly the opposite is true . The fact that our monitoring systems
picked it up and the way in which the system s respond are things th at we should salute,
and we should be proud of the response that  occurred and the way that incident was
dealt with. Then we had another one of thes e Labour attempts to sort of rewrite the
history. Let me go through. He said that this is just like what occurred in the building
and mining industry regulatory setting. Well, I would love to quote in terms of the
building law reform, Mr O’Connor, the wo rds of George Hawkins, one of his
colleagues. Do you know what George Hawkin s said? He said “How dare the National
Party claim credit for the build ing liberalisation that occurred  in 1991.” He said that all
of this is Labour’s work.
Hon Damien O’Connor: Tongue in cheek.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Well, no, actually. For the record, Mr O’Connor, the
building law reform was introduced by the fourth Labour Government. The bill was
introduced by Margaret Austi n, and actually it had its th ird reading only after the
change of Government.
I have a question on mining. Mr O’Connor wa nts to highlight the mining. I have a
simple question for him: duri ng his 9 years in Government , from 1999 to 2008, if he
was so wise about the deficiencies in th e mining industry regulations, why did Labour
do absolutely nothing for 9 years? You know  what really is the issue with Mr
O’Connor? Mr O’Connor will play  petty politics over the 29 tragic dead miners on the
West Coast, just in the same way as he will play petty politics with the issue of
biosecurity, rather than actually making sure that this country has the right systems and
the right rules around protecting our vital industries.
I want to also talk about the issue of Smar tGate. It is interes ting, Mr O’Connor, that
we have just had a review of SmartGate. That member repeatedly stood up in the House
and said that SmartGate would increase th e biosecurity risk for New Zealand. Do you
know what the review shows? Actually, they are getting more and improving New
Zealand’s biosecurity. It is de livering better biosecurity results in the audit that has just
been published 3 weeks ago, showing again the success of this Government.
The last point I want to challenge Mr O’Connor and the Labour Party on is this
playing politics. Whether it be in terms of the capsicums, the pork, the honey, or the
tomato, we on this side of th e House say that our biosecurit y decisions need to be made
on the basis of good risk management and scie nce, not politics—not politics. You see,
we have had an age-old argument—90 years going—in respect of access for apples into
Australia. We are a country that makes our living out of exporting biological products in
markets overseas, and we cannot have a double standard, saying in one breath that when
Australians come to make decisions about New Zealand apples a nd managing the risk
of fire blight, we want an independent, sc ience-based approach, and then when it comes
to New Zealand on the other foot, and it comes to issues of pork or capsicums or honey
or any other, we are going to take a political and not a science-based approach.
Hon Damien O’Connor: It’s not based on science, Nick.
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5181

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I say to Mr O’Connor that what  he is effectively arguing is
that the decisions about those biosecurity and import standards should be made by
political representatives, rather than by scientists, and we on this side of the House, as a
party that stands for trade and for earning this country’s living from biological products,
say that our biosecurity systems need to be first class, and our decisions about import
standards need to be based on science, not politic s. That is what this bill is about. This
Government is proud of the work that we are doing in biosecurity. It is part of what we
are doing to build a better future for this country.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I want everyone to know
that the contribution just given by Dr Nick Smith demonstrates that the only knowledge
he has about biosecurity is a knowledge of the clever root weevil, an experience the man
can no doubt elaborate upon at a given point in time. Perhaps he might be a bit more at
home, however, talking about th e sea squirt or anything, beca use no one on this side of
the House is playing petty politics. He is such a senior parliamentarian, and I accept that
there has been a bit of peevishness in the House today, and I accept that he has been
through somewhat of a torrid time, which I can  relate to myself. But I say do not bring
into the House in a debate the names or the fact that we have su ffered those fatalities.
You are better than that, Dr Smith. This is about the quality of our systems to ensure
that the primary produce owners can continue to invest into the future. Do not allow
your rhetoric to cause you to fail to live up to your own standards as a senior
parliamentarian, which you are more than capable of maintaining.
So we will support this bill, the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill. We are of the view,
however, that the Government, for reasons that it understands  better than perhaps we
do, did cut into the available budget, and we feel, as we have said on numerous
occasions, that that weakens the ability of those who are guardians at the edges of the
State to actually maintain our standards. About two-thirds of the general primary
produce merchandise sector, etc. , actually is at stake here. I accept that that member
does come from a part of New Zealand where there is the vestiges of a pipfruit industry.
Without a doubt, if we continue to allow a nd observe and even respond to Dr Smith’s
contributions, we will be not only worsening his reputation but lessening the tone of the
debate.

items.speaker: The guts of the debate is this
items.text: although we will support the Biosecurity Law Reform
Bill, there are sections we remain mightily concerned about. It is the right of every
parliamentarian to continue to point out that you cannot cut indiscriminately. Every time
that we point out that indiscriminate cuts  are at stake here, the Government hopes to
cause us to have to defend our preference for spending money. In actual fact, it is an
investment in the largest si ngle contributing sector to ou r exports. Without exports to
borrow their own narrative, there is no grow th in GDP, because the Government has
shrivelled and shrunk the size of the domestic economy as it pursues excessive levels of
austerity, etc.—freeze the regions, forget about  the regions. Whether it is in transport,
whether it is in the ports sector, whether it is in the manufacturing sector, what are we
left to fall back upon? We fall back upon t hose very types of produce that need very
good sector protection.
It could be said that it sounds slightly trivialising to talk about sniffer dogs, but
without a doubt those of us who travel freque ntly are often very happy to see the sniffer
dogs going about their business. The fact that only one new sniffer dog has been
produced suggests that there are no pest dangers  coming back, or that it has become too
expensive. Often the public need to see a symbol or something that epitomises the
miserly, foolish approach taken by the current Government. If you looked at the money
that has been wasted in putting together  the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment, those funds would be better de dicated to the men and women who work
5182 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012
inordinately long hours, etc. doing a difficult  job, because you are dealing with people
who are often offended, and who are often fright ened or confused as they come into our
country. Those biosecurity staff need to be re warded. They need to be talked up. They
do not need to be sold out.
On this side of the House we are very conscious of not only the work they do, but the
inordinate amount of investment at stake. Sure, that side of the House is arguing that we
live in austere times. We are suffering the ongo ing effects of the global financial crisis.
But you will have no economy unless you continua lly remain alert, and send a constant
message, as the changing nature of our ow n population grows, that when you come to
our country, not only are these the rules, but your wrongdoing, your foolishness, or your
ignorance will not go undetected. Those ar e welcome and obvious contributions that
should be coming into this debate—not thes e very shallow and loud remarks coming
from the member as he watches my good fr iend Sam Lotu-Iiga beat him back into
Cabinet. But that is another matter. We do not want to stir up the prospect that we might
suffer, God forbid, a foot-and-mouth s care—a foot-and-mouth experience—but I
remind the members on the other side of th e House, as one of my colleagues said
earlier, that there was a certain moth. Just look at the tragedy that befalls, unfortunately,
a lot of our wh ānau. There is a disproportiona tely large element of M āori investment in
the kiwifruit industry, so we know personally, even in that part, which is often not
thought of as a key contributor to the pastoral sector or th e horticultural sector, of the
dangers and the downsides.
How can the current administration genuine ly believe that it is going to grow—
whatever flash name it uses, partnership engagements, etc.—by throwing money at the
meat industry, the wool industr y, and various other elements of the pastoral sector if
they are going to cut the most valuable thin  line of resistance? It cannot escape the
mathematics. It may seek to justify that, but all we have got to do is remind it of that
unwanted Australian, otherwis e known as the Queensland fruit fly. I am disappointed
that Dr Nick Smith did not focus on the fruit fly. No doubt the man could expand at
length—[Interruption] Well, I have got to tell you, once you stand and you make the
silly mistake of invoking the names or the f act that fatalities have been suffered, and
you try to sheet that home to a member on th is side of the House, then shame on Nick
Smith for diminishing the quality of this debate and being so foolhardy as to do that as a
senior parliamentarian. I do not, in the short term, intend to allow him to forget that.
But on to the other elements of the bill. I have an orientation towards supporting a lot
of self-regulation, but in this case we cannot allow t hose who are advocates of self-
regulation to enjoy all of the responsibility without any clea r direction, and, in addition
to that, with the right balance between who will pay, because they will bear the costs if
they get it wrong. I think it is a legitimate political debate and it is a legitimate
philosophical debate as to what extent th e State can hand out. I happen to think that
Judith Collins, on the matter of alcohol, has probably got it wrong, because there will be
no adequate self-regulation in the alcohol indus try, but we will sort that into the future.
There is a case for self-regulation here in th e meat industry, but, as  my colleague said,
we cannot back it indiscrimina tely in the event that there is no overarching direction or
there is not an adequacy of res ources. But that is not to say that they should not be able
to come and advocate—not so much only on th e basis of historical experience overseas,
but with genuine data and science.
I actually have a great deal of sympathy for what the pork industry is currently
saying. Unfortunately, I doubt wh ether it will make much im pact on this particular
administration. That is not to say that the current Minister for Primary Industries is
pigheaded or anything like that. But once they  set their sight on a course of action, we
have here in many cases amongst the senior Cabinet Ministers a le vel of intransigence
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5183
that they will not turn. They seem to seek to ape the excesses of Margaret Thatcher or
something like that. Unfortunately, I have very little confidence that the pork industry is
going to not so much get its way but be able  to make an impact. As my colleague has
said, it is providing genuine data. It is pr oviding genuine scientific information. Perhaps
it has been lost in the swirl that passes for— well, not even the swirl, but the torpor of
the bureaucracy, etc.
But in that lies an exact example as to why, yes, you can support self-regulation to a
certain level, but in the absence of an overarching direction and in the absence of
adequate resources, not only ar e we putting our key contributo rs to our export sector at
risk, but we are actually dimi nishing the underlying worth of the principle—i.e. that the
State does not need to do everything, but th e State cannot yield unless there is an
adequate level of resource and a clear overa rching direction. Despite these misgivings,
we will continue to support the bill. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: The Green Party, unfort unately, is opposing the
Biosecurity Law Reform Bill. This bill does not go nearly far enough, and even if it did,
this bill is not being resourced well enough. We  would need some significant changes,
which have not come through the select committ ee process at all. There are parts of the
bill that we can see could have benefits. Extending our reach to the exclusive economic
zone is consistent with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and would
ratify the international conventions for ship ballast water, and there are some immediate
benefits there. Establishing a national policy direction would make the Crown be bound
to regional pest plans—and we may speak to th at a bit more because that is flawed as
well—but the theory behind it is all good.
I turn to distributed re sponsibility for biosecurity  management. Biosecurity
management would be less centralised, with new duties placed on the importers to
proactively manage the risks. But that leaves  a huge hole as well, particularly when our
inspections are under-resource d. Industry groups can beco me management agencies
with significant powers to make decisions a nd raise levies. There is a benefit here. The
new agencies would be subject to the Offici al Information Act and we may actually get
some real inside stuff on whether or not th ey are working. But I would suspect that
some of the sectors will be reluctant to be open to that level of scrutiny and may be
reluctant to join in to some of those agreem ents that the Government is trying to put on
to them. The new biosecurity information da tabase will mean that personal, land, and
biosecurity data will be collected and shared, enabling better risk management in the
future. So there are some positive things.
However, there are a number of other parts of  the bill that are ve ry concerning to us,
and we cannot support the bill. Targeted risk management seems like a good idea at first
glance, and, yes, we do need to target  our limited resources  in the best way.
Recognising the huge size of the biosecurity task, this bill a ttempts to prioritise scarce
resources—and they are becoming scarcer all the time as this Government keeps
shrinking back on biosecurity. All of the G overnment’s current activity leads to these
resources being targeted at the cash co ws of the economy, while ignoring other,
vulnerable industries. The big economic cash cows of the moment may not be the big
cash cows in the future, and the shortcomings  in this bill and the huge shortcomings in
the resourcing of biosecurity by this Govern ment stand to leave a legacy for ongoing
generations. We can think of the pests that ha ve come in in recent  years that are here,
that are not going away, and that future generations have to factor in for their
management in primary industries. I can point out a few.
In the marine area Undaria costs the marine aquaculture industry significantly, and it
hooked into it and did something about it. But Undaria is here to stay, and it is
spreading as we speak. Yep, we may take an opportunity out of that and grow Undaria
5184 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012
for some markets—probably markets in th e countries where it came from—but at the
same time it is a massive cost. Pacific oyster—the way that was spread around
supported by a previous Minister of Fisheries, Sir Doug Kidd, who helped with that one.
The South African brown mussel was brought on a ship into Tasman Bay. Some of the
sea squirts, and there are more by the year in our marine environment. Kiwifruit—well,
we know all about kiwifruit and the Psa, th e pollen imports that came in so recklessly
and were allowed by this Government. The ki wifruit industry, of course, is subject to
huge risk by fruit fly and other potential pests as well.
The import health standard for capsicum, eggplant, tomatoes, cucumbers, and all of
those things was just mentioned before by Labou r. The risk of fruit fly getting into that
industry—and a number of the other fruit industries—is immense. To be actually
allowing the possibility and accepting a certain number of eggs coming in as a measure,
as a baseline, for biosecurity is appalling. We have already got the psyllid, which has
come in and has thrashed that industry, an d is causing huge amounts of pesticide to be
used that was not being used before. It is the same with th e potato industry—$250
million already down the tubes because of biosecurity shortfalls by this Government.
We could have used that $250 million in biosec urity to prevent othe r things getting in.
We know that if the fruit fly gets into the Bay of Plenty, they anticipate $820 million
will be lost, with 3,500 jobs down the tubes because of it. But ma ybe that is already
halfway down because of the slackness around the pollen and the Psa. In Hawke’s Bay
roughly $390 million will be down the tubes if fr uit fly gets in, with 3,000 jobs gone. In
Nelson it will be $265 million and almost 2,000 jobs are anticipated to be lost as well.
And then there is the honey. We anticipate,  because of the free-trade agreements,
allowing honey imports from Australia wi th known risk, with known disease factors
that we do not have in New Zealand alrea dy. That means a lot more chemicals being
used around our hives and a reduction in the quality of the produce that we want to send
overseas. I will just mention, by the way, with capsicum, eggplant, tomatoes, cucumber,
potatoes—things affected by th e psyllid, particularly the Solanums—there is a huge
amount of pesticide being used. Those i ndustries were getti ng better and better,
particularly the glasshouse industry, at not using dangerous pesticides on our kai, on our
food. But what has happened now? They were using biological controls and they were
very good managers, very efficient managers, bringing in insects th at would deal with
the pests that they had at the time, which were  the other form of white fly, aphis, mites,
and things. They were all under control thr ough using biological means. We have got
the psyllid. It is costing us as a community and in health, because if we test that
produce—if we dare to test that produce at the moment—we will always find significant
chemical residues, and not just one but a multiplicity of residues in that produce,
because they have not got a solution for psyllid.
We have to get on top of biosecurity better th an this bill is setting up. It is setting up
purely to alleviate the Government some money in looking after biosecurity. It is
looking after the cash cows. It is forgetti ng about the other indus tries out there, the
flower industry, the pork industry, and the honey industr y—those other ones that the
Government seems to think are too small to worry about—which may be the Zespris
and the Fonterras in the future if things go wrong in those industries. Our trees, our
forest industry, are also at significant risk, and the huge cost to the community when we
spray them when there is a gypsy moth outbreak is not acceptable.
The other thing with this bill is it does not really deal with the risks of genetic
engineering and the risks of contamination that  are inevitable if we have GE getting in
in the wrong way in this country. There ar e people who do not understand the depth of
the cost of that to New Zealand and to Br and New Zealand if we get it wrong in terms
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5185
of imports and contamination through seed, whether it be canola, corn, or something
else that has not appeared here as yet.
Lastly, this bill specifically makes biosecurity law subject to the limitation of
international trade agreements. That is terr ible. We lose our sovereignty on how we can
look after biosecurity in this country for future generations. Thank you. Unfortunately,
the Green Party will not be able to support this bill.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: It occurs to me that we have lost our
way with this debate somewhat. I think that the debate here relates to a piece of
legislation, the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill, that in my view is a very good piece of
legislation. The amount of money you put be hind a piece of legislation is quite a
different issue, and clearly the Greens, particularly, have lost sight of that fact. I think
this piece of legislation is a very good piece of legislation. It has been very well-
thought-out over a long, long time, and so I do not think we should ever lose sight of the
fact that we have such a piece of legisl ation. How we fund it is another matter. I
certainly support the way this Government is funding it, because at the end of the day
$750 million is a fairly significant slice of cash to put behind a biosecurity system.
We also should realise that we live in an  isolated place, probably one of the most
isolated agricultural producing countries in the world, so we are halfway to protecting
ourselves naturally by the ty ranny of distance. The other th ing, however, that I guess to
some extent circumvents that is the fact that we have one of the largest coastlines in the
world. It is clearly impossible for us to guara ntee we are going to protect our coastline,
however much money we put into it and however much resource we put into it.
This piece of legislation is probably one of  the most important pieces of legislation
this House will put through in this term of Parliament. There is some groundbreaking
change in this. It is the modernisation of a system. It allows those of us who wish to
travel to travel—provided we do not ta ke extra stuff in our bags—much more
efficiently, effectively, and quickly than we us ed to. It also allows, through much better
systems, the identification of risks to our economy, and the biosecurity system can pick
that up.
This Biosecurity Law Reform Bill is intended to provide a more efficient and
effective biosecurity system. It provides fo r partnerships where applicable and allows
for the fleet-footedness of our border contro l. Not every industry in New Zealand is
going to be able to participate in this part nership. There are some that clearly do not
have the structure to join partnerships w ith the Government, and I guess the equine
industry is one of those, wh ere it is spread right thr oughout New Zealand and does not
have a body that could coordinate  it. So that is a challenge for the future for pieces of
legislation such as this.
During the course of our hist ory we have had some spectac ular success, really, at
dealing with incursions in the past, with one of those being the scra pie disease. It came
to New Zealand about 20 or 30 years ago. We managed to  remove that from the
country. It did no further damage to our livesto ck industry at all. More recently we had
the equine flu in Australia, which was kept  from New Zealand by a very effective and
efficient border control system. So we do ha ve a border control sy stem that works. A
biosecurity—

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Oh, come on. What about the Psa virus?

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: Well, if you bring it in in your su itcase you will always get it in,
will you not? We have a border control system  and a biosecurity system that I think
works extremely effectively and if people wish  to try to shyster the system, they will
always be able to get through a system, b ecause no system is bulletproof. But I think
this bill puts in place a very strong system—a system that certainly complements the
way we want to operate in New Zealand in  the future. The trick for any business—in
5186 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012
fact, for the Government—is to get the balan ce between risk and re ward correct in the
pursuit of a healthy economy and a better outcome for our country . I was not on the
select—

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: If you start employing people and employ more biosecurity staff,
that would be a better outcome.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: We also banned parrots quite some time ago from this country—I
am not sure how he got here. I was not on the select committee that dealt with this
business when it first came before the House but I certainly have no problem in
supporting the third reading of this bill and I am sure it will be a great success for the
future of New Zealand. Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I am pleased to rise on behalf of New Zealand
First to take a call on this the third reading, the final act, we could say, of the great
theatre by which the Biosecurity Law Reform  Bill becomes law. New Zealand First is
opposed to the passage of this legislation, not  because we do not ag ree with the stated
aims of the bill—we do agree with them; there is fine intention within this bill—and not
because there are not good aspects to the b ill or there are not good elements within it.
The extension of New Zealand’s biosecurity laws and the abili ty to enforce them to the
200-mile exclusive economic zone is a good thing. Measures that will prevent unwanted
organisms from entering our waters via the ballast tanks carried by cargo ships are a
good thing.
The omnibus provisions of the bill bring several other Acts  of this Parliament, as
they relate to biosecurity, under one umbr ella. That is a good thing. But there are
exasperating elements to this bill also. I am  prompted to bring to the attention of the
House the North American groundhog, Marmota m onax. It is a squirrel-like creature, a
ground squirrel, a rodent of the family Sciuri dae. It is known in  some parts of the
United States as, variously, the land beav er, the woodchuck, and on occasion even the
whistle-pig—the whistle-pig. I am given cau se to wonder whether, if one gives a
whistle to a pig, it is still a pig. But I digress—I digress perhaps just a little.
I mentioned Marmota monax because it is the inspiration for a film. It is a funny film
starring Bill Murray, who is a funny man.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: What’s it called?

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Groundhog Day . In the film, which strangely enough is
entitled Groundhog Day, Bill Murray’s character relives the same day over and over. It
is this that reminds me of this bill. Bill Mu rray is a funny man; he is a funny Bill. This
bill is not a funny bill. It is not funny, because, just like in the film, when we look at this
bill, we are faced with the same sense of déjà vu as Bill Murray’s character experiences
throughout the story. Here we go again; that is  the theme of the movie. Once again, this
Government, this National Government, ha s correctly identified a problem—indeed, a
set of problems—and then gone about creating a bill that will entirely fail to properly
address them. All too often this Government does this. This Government creates
legislation that takes entirel y the opposite approach to pr oblems from that which is
required in order to solve them. It is th e same thing and it keeps happening over and
over. We are trapped in our own Groundhog Day with this bill and others of this
Government’s creation.
There are other eerie parallels between the groundhog and this bill. Its various names
have a curious relevance to aspects of this bill and to the way in which they will impact
on New Zealand’s biosecurity. Members may think I am taking a rather odd approach to
this third reading by drawing numerous refe rences to a rather  odd North American
rodent. I believe it is wholly appropriate b ecause it is reflective of this Government’s
rather odd approach to biosecurity, which is at the heart of this bill’s failings.
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5187
I reiterate, and we are happy to acknowledge , that there are good things within this
bill, and its stated intent is a good one. But at  the heart of its failings is the moving of
the focus of biosecurity away from direct inspections and towards a targeted regime
based on risk assessment and profiling. New Zealand First regards this approach as
deeply flawed. We know from experien ce—everyone in New Zealand knows from
experience—that, with the best will in th e world, we cannot stop every last pest or
disease or other biosecurity threat from cr ossing our borders. But with proper vigilance
we can minimise the threat of an incursion.  Even with full inspection, we know that
something going wrong is a case of not if but of when, and without proper vigilance and
full inspection, it becomes a case of not when but  of how soon. If we drop our guard in
this ill-advised manner, something will go wrong and something will  get in—than that
there is nothing more certain.
How does this relate to the groundhog? Well, as I mentioned before, one of its names
is woodchuck. There is a we ll-known tongue-twister that asks the question how much
wood a woodchuck could chuck under various circumstances. The answer in New
Zealand’s case might very well be none at al l, if our lax approach  to biosecurity means
that we let in a moth or a vi rus that devastates our pine fo rests. Without trees there will
be no wood for the woodchuck to chuck, no revenue from forest ry, and no jobs for
forestry workers either. Do we really want to open ourselves up to that sort of risk?
The whistle-pig is another name for the groundhog. And whistling forlornly for non-
existent pigs might be all that remains for our pork industry if inadequate safeguards at
the border mean that we allow the porcine  reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus
to enter and establish itself here. The land beaver—I do not even wish to begin drawing
comparisons between this bill and any so rt of beaver, however appropriate the
connotation might be. Suffice to say, in moving  the focus of biosecurity inspection in
the way that this bill would bring about, we are virtually admitting that not only do we
expect the horse to bolt but that we are le aving the stable door open to make its escape
even easier. And shifting res ponsibility for compliance from Government to industry is
yet another example of the type of self-regulation that we have seen so often and that we
know does not work. We have had leaky build ings, we have had Pike River, and now
this bill will deliver us foot and mouth dise ase—not if, but when. You can take that to
the bank.
New Zealand First supports calls from acr oss the primary production sector for the
100 percent inspection of all goods crossing the border and for th e screening of all
passengers, regardless of who they are and where they are travelling from. We salute the
Government’s intentions where this bill is  concerned, and we really wish it had been
able to get it right. But, just like Groundhog Da y, here we go again: it has not. This is a
deficient bill that will cost New Zealand d early and irrevocably, and New Zealand First
does not support it. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: After 23 years in the dairy industry and 15
years as a fish exporter, I am very, ve ry aware of our dependence on effective
biosecurity measures. But I would like to sp eak, in relation to this Biosecurity Law
Reform Bill, on pest control—pest control. Th is bill is worthy of support and I am very
glad to hear it is gett ing cross-party support, particularly from our friends in the Labour
Party. I am sorry that New Zealand First, a lthough praising the bi ll, cannot see fit to
support it, and it is a disappointment that th e Greens, although they support it, do not
actually come up to the bar and get in behind it.
However, in terms of the pest control aspect , my interest in this particular bill is
concentrated on the way it affects other enac tments, and one in particular is Part 3,
clause 79, “Amendment to Ombudsmen Act 1975”. Just to quote: “Part 2 of Schedule 1
of the Ombudsmen Act 1975 is amended by inserting ‘Management agencies under
5188 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012
Biosecurity Act 1993, if they ar e corporate bodies, in their role under pest management
plans or pathway management plans’ …” will be affected.
I am advised that the effect of this will be  to ensure that the Animal Health Board
will be subject to the Official Information Act. This has long been a request of the
people of the West Coast and Tasman and I am very pleased to be able to announce it to
them this evening—as long as the bill passes . I am grateful to the Minister for the
inclusion in this particular bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: As a former member—an alumnus—of
the Primary Production Committee for 6 years,  but not a current member, I was not
going to take a call in this debate, because this  is a very important piece of legislation,
until I heard the contribution of that well-known diplomat Ni ck Smith. I can talk about
this, because I am going to respond to the scu rrilous speech that he made in this House.
This is a bill about biosecurity. Tradi tionally, the Primary Production Committee,
chaired formerly by my colleague Damien  O’Connor and now by Shane Ardern, has
always been a committee that has been bipartisan. I remember one colleague—I think it
was David Carter; I am sure my colleague  Damien O’Connor will recall this—in the
select committee saying when they were in  Opposition: “We know we’re going to lose
on this, but we’re going to make our points. We’re going to ensure that the legislation
coming out of the Primary Production Comm ittee, which is vital to our primary
industries, comes to this House in as good a shape as it can be, because our primary
industries are so important to us.”
So this legislation is generally non-partisan  and there have been some non-partisan
contributions tonight, apart from the scurr ilous contribution—the scurrilous, low-life
contribution—from Nick Smith. What Nick Smith did, which had nothing to do with
this bill, was accuse my colleague Damien O’Connor, the member for the West Coast,
of playing politics with the tragedy that ha ppened at Pike River. That speech by Nick
Smith will stand in infamy. I acknowledge my colleague Damien O’Connor, and I think
it is appropriate to also ac knowledge Chris Auchinvole and other politicians who were
in and around that tragedy, ju st like the Canterbury earthquakes and other tragedies that
we have had. I think, beyond politics, people responded as best they could in a non-
partisan way to assist their communities, to  put an arm around those who had lost loved
ones, to express their love and affection for those communities, and to support them.
And for that scurrilous member, Nick Smith—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I understand what the member is doing, but all
members are honourable members. The use of that kind of adjective against the member
is out of order.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: That honourable member—ha, ha—Nick Smith
showed scurrilous behaviour in this House tonight, and this is a serious issue. He
brought a member into disrepute and made a scurrilous series of accusations that my
colleague played politics with  people’s lives and played politics with a tragedy. His
electorate borders the West Coast, and if anybody in their whole entire career has
played politics over and over and over again, whether it be ACC, whether it be a whole
host of issues, and wallowed in the gutter— the political gutter—it is the Hon Dr Nick
Smith.
I stand here in defence of my colleague , and in defence of and alongside Chris
Auchinvole and the other colleagues who went down to Pike River, along with leaders
in the community, and who stood by those men and women who lost loved ones. And if
they are watching tonight, I a pologise on behalf of this Pa rliament for the despicable
speech and accusation that that member, Ni ck Smith, made—and on the back of the
Biosecurity Law Reform Bill.
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5189
So Nick Smith’s intent was not to get up and talk about a bill that was in any way
connected to that series of tragedies; it was to get up on any piece of legislation and put
the boot into a colleague, but in doing so trample over the memories, the tragedy, and
the emotions of those people who lost loved ones in that tragedy.
Politicians get accused of a lot. Sometimes, yeah, we are a bit nasty. Sometimes we
do put the slipper into each other, and sometimes we do get a bit passionate, but, by
God, there was a colleague of mine who talk ed about the fact that there are written
Standing Orders and there are unwritten standi ng orders. The unwritten standing orders
are basically protocols between members of Parliament where there is a line that you do
not cross. I am glad the member is here. I am  glad he is here, with his hair standing on
end and his red face. I am glad he is here to listen, because that member’s behaviour has
been scurrilous. There is a lot said in this Chamber. As I have sa id, the slipper goes in
from time to time, but it has been—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: Attack the issue.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I will attack the issue, all right. The issue is that of
a member of Parliament coming into this Ch amber, using a basically bipartisan piece of
legislation to accuse another member of pl aying politics with those who died in a
tragedy—died in a tragedy.
|Hon Dr Nick Smith: It was Mr O’Connor who raised the issue of Pike.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: And here we go, because Dr Nick Smith—I am
glad he is here—shows no remorse in tramp ling over the spirit and memory of those
people who were lost.
That member is a sort of political version of a limbo dancer. He will go as low as he
can in this House, and he did tonight—ove r a biosecurity bill. It would not have
mattered whether it was a bill on anything. He got up to talk about biosecurity, to put
the slipper in. Well, I am going to move to the legislation, because that member is not
worth it. But I do apologise to those watching, because that member tonight has brought
this Chamber into disrepute, lowered the tone, and wallowed in the political sewer
where he treads very, very often—[Interruption] Very, very often.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: Who’s in the sewer?

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Oh, so I am accused of th at. No, I am accused of
standing up and defending a colleague from a vicious and scurrilous attack by that piece
of work over there.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: Who started it?

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Well, there you go! There is the second one. I
could forgive that member, because she has not been around here that long, and she is
not that experienced, and these things ha ppen, but, oh no, not that one over there—the
member for Nelson. He knew exactly what he was doing, exactly what he was saying. It
was calculated and it is seen for what it is.

items.speaker: We move to the legislation. I say this
items.text: we  will, as Damien O’Connor said, support
this piece of legislation, but with some gross reservations. Because, of course, this
legislation has been around for a while, dr essed up, brought into the Chamber, and
trumpeted in a lofty way that the National Pa rty does. But then we look at the history
and the facts. We know that Dr Nick Smith is great at getting up and lecturing us on
history and lecturing us  on what other Governments have done. But, you see, on entry
into this place in Government, what Nick Smith’s Government did was cut—
immediately in its first Budget—$2.8 million out of the biosecurity budget. That was its
commitment to biosecurity. We know, on all sides of this House, because we support
our primary industries, that an incursion of  any kind, whether it be  a minor incursion,
or, God forbid, whether it be foot-and-mouth, or whatever, would be terminal for our
primary industries in New Zealand.
5190 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012
Then it followed, of course , that in 2009 Dr Smith’s G overnment slashed 54 front-
line biosecurity officers. More redundancies have followed, and the latest figures show
there are 91 fewer staff on our borders now th an in 2008. So such is its commitment to
biosecurity. Then we talk about the biosecurity dogs, th e sniffer dogs. I do not think
Wellington Airport has had a sniffer dog, I think, since Oc tober—over a year ago. So
such is the Government’s commitment to bi osecurity. So, yes, we will support the bill,
but we know, of course, that if New Zeal and had an outbreak of foot-and-mouth, it
would cost us billions and b illions of dollars. It would destroy our primary industries
and destroy our economic base.
So I say to Dr Smith and others, as they stand here and lecture us on history, that
they should look at their own r ecent history in respect of thei r last few years in office,
and their commitment to biosecurity. There are many farmers on that side. There are
many farmers who are in the industry, doing the business, who know far more about this
sort of thing than many of us in this place who are townies.
But there is a commitment that is needed, a real one, not a piece of legislation that is
dressed up, but some dollars, some cents, and so me staff to protect our border. This is
what this is about, and this is  about “New Zealand Inc.” This  is not about politics. This
is about a bipartisan approac h, as we have generally had, to primary industries in this
country. So I say we should get a bit real a bout this. We should make a serious attempt
to get to grips with this a nd protect our border. We should not engage in scurrilous and
underhanded political sewer tactics, which we saw tonight from that member, Nick
Smith.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: I rise to support the Biosecurity
Law Reform Bill in its third reading. In doing so, I want to remind the House that I am a
new member to this House, and I am not goi ng to therefore dignify  the contribution of
the member who has preceded me with a resp onse, other than to say that, as a new
member, I know that that is the kind of speech that makes the public who are listening
to and watching this presentation on TV toni ght roll their eyes and wonder what it is
that we do in this House.
Here we are, debating importa nt legislation—important le gislation that goes to the
very root of supporting our primary industr ies and the very basis of our economy and
prosperity for the future. So, because we live in challenging, global times and a
challenging global environment, and because we have been so reliant over so many
years—in fact, our entire history—on the vi rtue of our distance and our position on the
globe as the main preventer and barrier to our biosecurity lapses, it comes now as being
very appropriate that this piece of legislation should co me before the House and be
passed this evening. I am delighted and thrilled  that it seems to have bipartisan support
across the House. That is a good thing—a very good thing.
I have the pleasure of repres enting a rural electorate—the very fine electorate of
Coromandel. In that electorat e, of course, horticulture, ag riculture—and all the cultures
for that matter—and aquaculture as well are all primary industries that are the backbone
of the Coromandel electorate. I know that in my electorate the communities in Katikati
and in Waih ī, and most recently in the area of Wh enuakite on the northern end of the
peninsula, have been plague d by the Psa drama that is  confronting our kiwifruit
industry. So biosecurity is important in my electorate and will continue to be so.
I am very pleased that this Governme nt is taking the a ppropriate action and
prevention measures that are required to ensure that our primary industries are protected
in a way that is effective going forward. I remember—it was only a few months ago—
the example that we had of the single Queensland fruit fly that was found in the urban
electorate of Mt Roskill. For me that proved that the system does work.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: It was Phil Goff.
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5191

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It was Phil Goff’s electorate, th at is right. But it was not Phil
Goff who was the fruit fly. So the system wo rked. It worked well, and for me it gives
me great confidence as a rural constituent member to support this bill. So I do so with
vigour and commend the bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a split call?

items.speaker: Rino Tirikatene
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: It is; right. A 5-minute call, Rino Tirikatene.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: I am pleased to make a short
contribution on the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill at its third reading. As I have
mentioned in my other contributions, biosecur ity is vitally important  to our country, to
our primary sectors. It is about protecting our industries, our regions, our brand, and our
pa. I use that descriptive term because it is a battle that goes on every day at our border,
where we have our visitors coming through our airports and goods that come through
our ports, and the flows that ha ppen every day. So it is an ongoing battle that goes on,
and we need the best biosecurity systems in the world.
I know that the Minister for Primary Industries does say that we do have a world-
class biosecurity system, and that must be the aspiration that we want to achieve.
Unfortunately, we have seen some really se rious mishaps, particularly over the past
couple of years, with some serious pest in cursions, as Mr Simpson has just spoken
about. We have had the Psa virus affecti ng the kiwifruit industry, and some other
serious incursions such as the fruit fly from Queensland.  The varroa bee mite was
another one that has come through.
We need to protect our pa, and Labour does support this legislation. We have
supported it right the way through. We have  expressed a lot of reservations around
particular things like the Government-i ndustry agreements, but on the whole we do
support the bill because there we re a lot of aspects around our biosecurity systems that
needed updating, amending, and improving, and they are incorporated into the bill,
which we have supported.
As Mr McKelvie mentioned, though, there can be the most elegantly drafted piece of
legislation that has all the bell s and whistles in it, but it is  actually the resourcing that
underpins that legislation that  is vitally important. So I do differ from Mr McKelvie
because it is the resourcing of our biosecur ity system that has faced significant cuts
under this Government. Hence we have h eavyweights from right across our primary
sector that have been really upset at the amount of cuts that have happened to the
biosecurity sector and right across the boar d. I am talking about organisations like
Federated Farmers, Horticulture New Zeal and, and New Zealand Kiwifruit Growers.
They have said that there n eed to be fundamental changes to the biosecurity system and
there needs to be more resourcing put into the system.
What we have seen under this current Gove rnment is a relaxing of our biosecurity
system. The Government wants to make things easier. It wants to make travel, tourism,
trade, and the importing of goods a lot easier fo r business, so it has lowered the cost of
our biosecurity system and our model, and it is putting more of an emphasis on risk
management rather than risk prevention. Well, if the Government listened to our
primary sector industries, which are saying we need to put the emphasis right on
protecting our pa, if it listened to Federa ted Farmers, and to those other esteemed
industry organisations that represent the prim ary sector, it would hear them saying that
we need to beef up the funding and the resourcing that goes into biosecurity.
We need only to look at things like what  the industry is calling for—100 per cent X-
ray checking of all baggage th rough all our airports, and sniffer dogs. We all travel
regularly in and out of Welli ngton Airport. I have not seen one little beagle sniffer dog
for years. We also need an increase in bi osecurity staff. We have seen a 12 percent
5192 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 12 Sep 2012
reduction in front-line biosecurity staff under this Government, yet we have seen a 14
percent increase in the amount of  international visitors, so there have definitely been
cuts to the resourcing of the biosecurity sy stem. So that is what we do challenge the
Government on.
We do understand that this piece of legislation is long overdue. A lot of the measures
in the legislation were created under the Labour Government, so we do commend this
bill at its third reading, but we implore the Government to further resource the
biosecurity sector.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: This evening there has b een a fair amount of self-
congratulation from some of the Governme nt members. I just want to begin by
correcting a logical error that has appeared in several of th eir speeches, and that is that
finding a pest, finding the Queensland fruit fly in Mount Roskill, is not evidence that the
system works. It is evidence that the system  is not a complete failure. We actually do
not know how good our system is. We do know th at there have already been some very
substantial and dangerous incursions, and that  we have ample evidence of the risk of
many others.
What I wanted to spend the bulk of my time on this evening was an aspect of this
issue of biosecurity that has not been explor ed in the debate toni ght on the Biosecurity
Law Reform Bill, and that is the importance of biosecurity not for our primary
industries but for our natural biodiversity. I have  said previously in debates on this bill
and on other biosecurity measures that the fl ora and fauna of this country are unique in
the world. If they do not survive here, they are lost to the world for ever. So the
consequences of biosecurity risks are not onl y to the primary industries—and I am sure
that everybody in the House shares concern ab out those—but also to the natural world,
and yet this bill and the measures it include s, and all of the thinking that underpins it,
have been largely silent on that issue.
Why is that a problem? It is a problem because of the consequence of targeting.
When we choose to target a par ticular set of measures or a particular set of issues, we
are implicitly choosing to de-t arget everything else. What th at means is that when we
target even more the primar y industries through this bill, we are placing even less
emphasis on the importance of protecting our natural biodiversity, and that is a major
problem. It is also a problem within the meas ures of the bill, because one of the things
that I anticipate and confiden tly predict will occu r under this bill is that with these
Government-industry agreements, those sectors that are able to afford a significant
investment into such agreements will be the ones that get the great treatment from our
biosecurity services, and those sectors that  cannot will not get that same service.
Conservation of our natural biodiversity will be at the very end of the queue.
But the consequences of this bill for conservation are worse still than those that I
have mentioned. One of the provisions of this  bill will bind the Crow n to regional pest
plans. That in and of itself is not a problem —in fact, it is probably a good thing to do—
but that new obligation, which will have at  the very least a multimillion-dollar impact
and liability on the Department of Cons ervation, does not come matched with the
funding to be able to meet that obligation. What it means is that, in addition to,
effectively, less protection from biosecurity risks for our conservation estate, for our
natural biodiversity—in addition to that problem—there will also be effectively a major
funding cut to the Department of Conservation, because funds that were intended to
protect our natural biodiversity through Vote Conservation will be lost to the sector. So
there will be multiple problems for conservation.
I want to finish by talking briefly about free trade, because it seems to me that in
many ways biosecurity is the victim of the obsession with free trade that seems to have
gripped this country—in several ways. No one argues that there is enough money to pay
12 Sep 2012 Biosecurity Law Reform Bill 5193
for all of the things that one  could possibly do to protect our country from biosecurity
risks. But, given unlimited ri sks that are proportional to the amount of stuff that we
import and limited dollars, the logical, rationa l response would be to take whatever
steps we can to restrict the imports. We do not do that, because of the obsession with
free trade. The Green Party opposes the bill.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: It is my great pleasure to take what I think
is the last call in this third reading debate on the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill. I want to
firstly thank Mr Mallard for re minding me before the dinner hour that every call slot is
precious. This bill has been well canvassed on its third reading, and I commend it to the
House.
